H6835.portee: The pitcher reminds us that God cares about the simple details of human life: water for drinking, oil for eating. It also symbolizes the trust of the poor and the servant: the widow possesses so little that her nearly empty pitcher of oil becomes the starting point of the miracle. These stories teach that God provides for our most basic needs and honors those who trust Him, even when provisions seem exhausted.

sens: The act of waiting for something with confidence
The state of one who looks forward with expectation
A feeling of anticipation directed towards deliverance or salvation
H6836.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes the action of watching, observing attentively while waiting for something. It is the attitude of one who looks from an elevated position to see what they hope for coming. In Lamentations 4:17, Israel "waited in vain for help": their eyes were turned toward a nation, hoping it would intervene — a disappointed expectation, as that nation did not deliver them. 2. The word then takes on the emotional sense of confident waiting, of hope. It is this blend of observance and hope: one looks toward the horizon because they expect something good, even if that something is not yet visible. 3. For the believer, hope becomes this orientation of the heart toward God, this confidence that God will act to deliver, save, or assist us.
H6836.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to look," "to observe," or "to watch." The underlying image is that of a sentinel posted on a watchtower, eyes fixed on the horizon to discern the approach of the one who is to come. This root appears in other Hebrew words denoting vigilant waiting. Hope is essentially this posture: looking steadfastly toward God or toward the awaited salvation.
H6836.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew text of the Bible (Lamentations 4:17). It is set in the painful context of besieged or exiled Israel, unable to find help from the nations. Their eyes consumed with waiting, but their hope was in vain. It is a human hope, directed toward earthly help that never came — which contrasts with biblical hope that must turn toward God alone and will never be disappointed.
H6836.portee: This text teaches a crucial lesson to the believer: hope placed in man, in a nation, or in any creature ultimately leads to disappointment. Lamentations 4:17 shows the consumed eyes of Israel who hoped in vain. The message for the Christian is that our true hope must be in God alone, who never abandons us. It is a call to turn our eyes away from false sources of help and fix them solely on the Lord.

sens: Son of Gad and founder of a lineage of Israel
H6837.detail: 1. Tsiphjon is one of the seven sons of Gad listed during Jacob's descent into Egypt (Genesis 46:16). He represents a branch of the tribe of Gad, which will be counted among the twelve tribes of Israel.
H6837.origine: The name Tsiphjon literally means "watchman" or "observer" (from the root meaning "to look," "to observe"). It is a typical name from the patriarchal generations, often reflecting an image or a notable trait. His brothers also bear Hebrew names: Haggi, Shuni, Etsbon, Eri, Arodi, and Areeli. The text of Numbers 26:15 also refers to him as Zaphon, a spelling variant of the same character.
H6837.emploi: Tsiphjon appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 46:16, in the genealogical list of the sons of Gad who accompany Jacob into Egypt. This list establishes the foundations of the twelve tribes and their family subdivisions. In Numbers 26:15, the same man is called Zaphon during the census of the people in the desert, showing that biblical genealogies sometimes use name variants while designating the same person. His role in sacred history is that of a patriarch: he gives his name to his descendants, the Tsiphjonites, who are part of the chosen people.

sens: A flat and thin pastry, round or oval in shape
A simple food made of flattened and baked dough
H6838.detail:
1. The word denotes a fine, flat pastry, similar to a wafer or unleavened bread — a cake without leaven, quickly cooked on a griddle or in an oven. This is the concrete and culinary sense of the term.
2. The manna, this miraculous food in the desert, is compared to this cake to give the Israelites an image of what they ate each day: something light, white like crystallized honey, that crumbled under the tooth. This comparison helps the reader to imagine the texture and appearance, and shows that the manna, though foreign, had nourishing and almost delicate qualities.
H6838.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of flattening or spreading: צפף (tsapaph). It is a feminine noun that retains the image of a dough that has been flattened and then baked. In the biblical world, flat unleavened cakes were common foods, quickly cooked on hot stones or in an oven.
H6838.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Exodus 16:31, where Moses explains to the Israelites the nature of the manna by comparing it to a fine, white pastry with a taste of honey. This unique description aims to make concrete and flavorful what this extraordinary food was, neither classic bread nor natural fruit, but something tender and delicate that fell each morning from heaven.
H6838.portee: This simple yet vivid comparison reminds us that God provides for our needs in a concrete and generous way. The manna was not coarse or tasteless food, but something good and nourishing: it shows the loving attention of the Father for His people in the desert, and His desire that we have what we need to live and be satisfied.

sens: Watchtower or observation place on a height
Location on Mount Pisgah in Moab, facing the Jordan Valley
Site where the diviner Balaam pronounced his oracles
H6839.detail: Tsophim literally means "the watchers" or "the observers" — a name that evokes a high place from which one can see far. It is a location on the summit of Mount Pisgah, in Moab, overlooking Israel. In Numbers 23:14, King Balak brings the diviner Balaam there to curse the people of Israel; Balaam builds seven altars there and, instead of cursing, he blesses Israel and prophesies. The name of the place corresponds to its function: it is a lookout point from which one dominates the land.
H6839.origine: The name comes from the root צפה (sâpha), which means "to look," "to observe," "to be a sentinel." It is a place named after what was done there — observing and watching over the territory from a high position. The plural suffix indicates that it refers to the "watchers" or a place of watchers.
H6839.emploi: Tsophim appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 23:14. It is the second place where Balak brings Balaam to curse Israel. Located on Pisgah, it provided Balaam with an overview of the camp of Israel. It is from this observation point that Balaam proclaims his second blessing prophecy — a key moment where, despite the strategic position given to Balaam to do harm, God compels his mouth to bless.
H6839.portee: This place reminds us that the plans of the powerful to do evil are futile in the face of God's sovereignty. Even positioned at the best observation post, equipped with all the rites of invoking occult power, Balaam can only bless those whom God has blessed. It is a lesson in trust: no human scheme has power over the people of God when they are under His protection.

sens: male of the goat
animal offered in sacrifice
H6841.detail:
1. The goat is the adult male of the domestic goat, a common livestock animal in the ancient Near East. It is distinguished from the female goat and the lamb by its strength and bulk.
2. In Israelite worship, the goat served as a sacrificial animal, particularly for sin offerings. In Ezra 6:17, during the dedication of the rebuilt temple, twelve goats are offered "as sin offerings for all Israel, according to the number of the tribes of Israel": each of these twelve animals represents one of the twelve tribes and symbolically bears its atonement.
H6841.origine: The Hebrew word צְפִיר comes from a root that evokes the idea of "smallness" or "relative weakness" — not that the goat is weak in itself, but perhaps because it was less prestigious than the ram in the hierarchy of sacrificial victims. The Aramaic word צְפִיר, used here in the book of Ezra, corresponds exactly to the Hebrew word צָפִיר (H6842), which shows the identity of the Aramaic language of the Levant at that time.
H6841.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezra 6:17, at the time when the second temple is completed and dedicated under Persian rule, about 70 years after the destruction of the first temple. The context shows that the goat, like the ram and the lamb listed at the same time, is part of the sacrificial system of Second Temple Judaism. The number twelve (one goat per tribe) emphasizes that each tribe of Israel, even when dispersed, is represented and concerned by the sin offering. It is an ordinary domestic goat, not the scapegoat of Yom Kippur, but an animal dedicated to the altar.
H6841.portee: This text reminds us that the people of God, even restored and weakened after exile, recognized their continual need for atonement and placed reconciliation with God at the heart of their worship. The sacrifice of goats, seemingly modest after the hundred bulls, illustrates how all members of the people, from the most powerful to the most humble, depend on God's atoning grace.

sens: Animal: the male of the goat
Sacrificial animal: victim offered for the atonement of sins
Prophetic figure: symbol of royal or political power
H6842.detail:
1. The goat is simply the adult male of the goat, recognizable by its size, strength, and often its imposing horns. It embodies virility and animal power.
2. In Israelite worship, the goat was offered in sin offerings to seek forgiveness for sins: it was regularly offered at the temple, as shown by the purification rituals of the kingdom and the sanctuary (2 Chronicles 29:21, Ezra 8:35). It is a valuable animal, chosen from the flocks for this solemn religious function.
3. The prophet Daniel sees in a vision a goat with a great horn that symbolizes the king of Javan (Alexander the Great and the Greek empire): the animal becomes a figure of dominant political and military power (Daniel 8:5, 8:21).
H6842.origine: The Hebrew word צָפִיר (tsaphir) comes from a root meaning probably "to leap" or "to bound," which suits the agile and energetic animal. A closely related Aramaic term, צְפִיר (tsephir), designates the same animal. The goat was well known in ancient Near Eastern societies for its utility (milk, meat, skin) and its place in religious rituals.
H6842.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, always in religious or prophetic contexts. In the historical books (2 Chronicles, Ezra), the goat figures among the sacrificial victims offered at festivals or for communal atonement. In the book of Daniel, particularly in chapter 8, the word takes on a symbolic meaning: the "goat" in a prophetic vision represents a powerful political empire, showing how a real animal can transform into an Old Testament image of royalty. The context determines each time whether the word refers to the concrete animal or its prophetic significance.
H6842.portee: The goat teaches the reader the reality of sacrifice for atonement: it is a living, precious animal that dies to purify the people of its faults. This image prepares the heart to understand the supreme sacrifice of Christ. In Daniel's visions, the goat reminds us that the political powers of the world, however imposing they may seem, remain images seen by the prophet and subject to God's eternal plan.

sens: That which surrounds, that which encircles something
Moment when it is someone's turn, period or instant that returns
Head ornament: crown, diadem, or adornment
Misfortune, calamity that approaches and whose moment has come
H6843.detail:
1. The primary meaning of the word describes something that surrounds: a crown, a diadem, or an adornment that encircles the head like a royal or sacred ornament (Isaiah 28:5, where the Lord becomes a "glorious diadem").
2. From this comes the meaning of turn: the moment that comes, the instant when it is someone's turn to pass, the period that arrives. It is as if time makes a turn until it reaches you.
3. This word also designates the crown or adornment itself, the ornament that encircles the head, often a symbol of royalty, dignity, or glory.
4. In Ezekiel, "your turn is coming" means that the moment of misfortune is approaching, that it is now the turn of trouble and judgment to come (Ezekiel 7:7 and 7:10). The idea remains one of succession: after peace comes your turn to suffer.
H6843.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to turn," "to make turn," or "to surround." The basic image is that of a crown turning around the head. The word belongs to the family of terms that express circularity and succession: what turns returns, what encircles delineates a moment or a turn. This notion of "turn" (moment that comes after others) naturally arises from the image of the circuit, of that which surrounds and returns.
H6843.emploi: This word appears three times in the Bible. In Isaiah 28:5, it designates the glorious adornment and crown of glory that the Lord will be for His people, in a context of restoration and beauty. In Ezekiel 7:7 and 7:10, it takes on a dark tone: "your turn is coming" announces the approach of the day of judgment and trouble for the land. The context of Ezekiel shows that this word can lose its royal crown luster to become the announcement of a succession of terrible events. The meaning oscillates between honor and calamity depending on the situation, but the central idea remains that of a moment that comes at its appointed time.
H6843.portee: This word reminds the reader that there is an order, a cycle of things: everyone has their moment, their turn. For those who await divine restoration, this turn can be a promise of crowning and adornment (Isaiah). For those who refuse God's call, this turn can become an inevitable judgment (Ezekiel). The word invites reflection on the progression of divine time and the reality that our actions have consequences.

sens: Action of staying awake and alert to monitor
Period of surveillance during the night
State of vigilance and preparation
H6844.detail:
1. The word designates the action of staying awake and alert to monitor something or someone, standing guard. In the context of Isaiah 21:5, a table is set while "the guard watches": the soldiers remain vigilant, attentive, ready to intervene in case of danger. It is an active and responsible vigilance.
2. By extension, it is also the period of surveillance, particularly that of the night when danger is greater and minds tend to sleep. It is the moment when someone must remain conscious and alert to protect.
3. The word also evokes a general state of spiritual or moral preparation and vigilance: being on watch means being ready, attentive, without allowing one's conscience to fall asleep.
H6844.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of "to keep" or "to be vigilant." It belongs to the family of words that describe surveillance and protection. The basic image is that of a watchman who does not sleep to fulfill his mission of surveillance.
H6844.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (Isaiah 21:5). It describes the guard that watches during the night, in a context of waiting before a battle or divine judgment. It is a rare term that emphasizes the importance of staying awake and vigilant in the face of significant events.
H6844.portee: This word reminds us that vigilance is a responsibility: the one who watches protects others and stands ready. For the Christian, it is also an invitation not to fall asleep spiritually, to remain aware and attentive to God's calls. Watching is an act of faithfulness and seriousness towards what has been entrusted to us.

sens: Put away, voluntarily conceal
Keep precious, preserve with care
Keep secret, withhold without revealing
Observe in secret, spy
Accumulate, store up
H6845.detail:
1. To hide something means to place it where it cannot be easily seen or found. This is what Moses' mother does in Exodus 2:2: she hides her son for three months to protect him from royal threat. The image is one of protection through secrecy.

2. To keep precious means to set aside like a treasure that one preserves. In Proverbs 2:1, being rich or wise means "to keep" one's precepts with oneself, as one keeps wealth. It is also to store up: the wicked accumulates goods (Job 15:20, "share") or the righteous accumulates wisdom (Proverbs 13:22).

3. To keep secret means not to reveal. In Proverbs 10:14, the wise "withholds" knowledge — he does not shout it from the rooftops like the fool. In Proverbs 2:7, God "reserves" salvation for the righteous.

4. To observe in secret means to spy, to watch while hiding. This is what enemies do in Psalms 56:7: they "spy" on the psalmist's footsteps to set traps for him. The meaning shifts from "to place in a hidden place" to "to hide oneself to observe."

5. To accumulate or reserve is also used figuratively: God "stores up" the days of judgment (Job 24:1), accumulating them for the moment when He will need them.
H6845.origine: The Hebrew root צפן (tsaphan) literally means "to put aside, relegate." It evokes the idea of placing something in a remote, hidden, protected place. The verb is used in the Qal (simple form) for "to hide, treasure," in the Niphal (passive form) for "to be hidden," and in the Hiphil (causative form) for "to cause to be hidden." The word belongs to the family of verbs of concealment and protection in Hebrew.
H6845.emploi: This verb appears 31 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the Wisdom Books (Job, Proverbs, Psalms). It primarily designates the action of hiding someone or something concretely: hiding baby Moses (Exodus 2:2), hiding Rahab the spies (Joshua 2:4). It then takes on a more spiritual and moral meaning: hiding a hidden intention, observing in secret, spying (Psalms 56:7, Proverbs 1:11). Finally, it describes accumulation and preservation: keeping wisdom within oneself (Proverbs 2:1, Psalms 119:11), putting aside — whether it be a share, a judgment, or a blessing (Job 15:20, Job 24:1, Proverbs 2:7). The word denotes both the action of protecting through secrecy and that of concealing malicious intentions.
H6845.portee: This word invites the reader to distinguish between two forms of "hiding": that which protects (Moses' mother, God who reserves His grace), and that which deceives (the enemies who spy, the wicked who secretly accumulate). It also urges to "keep" actively the Word of God in one's heart, not as a passive possession, but as a living treasure entrusted to memory and conscience. It is a call to be on the side of those who protect, preserve, and meditate on divine truth, rather than those who hide to do evil.

sens: high-ranking priest at the temple in Jerusalem during the reign of King Zedekiah
H6846G.detail: Zephaniah is the name of an important priest who served at the temple during the time of the last king of Judah before the fall of Jerusalem. He held the rank of "second priest" — the title that comes directly after the high priest — and played a trusted role with King Zedekiah. The royal authorities send him as a delegate to the prophet Jeremiah to intercede on behalf of the kingdom (Jeremiah 37:3). He also receives a letter from Jeremiah addressed to the temple clergy (Jeremiah 29:25-29), and he is prominent enough to ensure its reading. When Jerusalem falls and Nebuchadnezzar takes the city, Zephaniah is among the captured priests: he is brought to Riblah with the high priest and other leaders of the worship (2 Kings 25:18, Jeremiah 52:24), and there he is executed.
H6846G.origine: The name Zephaniah means "the Lord has treasured" or "the Lord has hidden": it comes from Hebrew roots expressing the idea of keeping, reserving. It is a name of trust, that of a person whom God kept under His protection — a poignant irony for this priest who will see the temple destroyed and perish himself during the capture of the city.
H6846G.emploi: Zephaniah appears six times in the Scriptures, only in the later historical books (2 Kings and Jeremiah), all between the siege of Jerusalem in 587 B.C. and its immediate consequences. In Jeremiah, we see the man in charge: the king dispatches him as a messenger to the prophet (Jeremiah 37:3, Jeremiah 21:1), and he receives correspondence from the prophet (Jeremiah 29:25-29). In 2 Kings 25:18 and Jeremiah 52:24, he appears at the moment of the final blow, taken into captivity. These last two verses recount exactly the same event in parallel: we know Zephaniah only by his swift action and his tragic end.
H6846G.portee: Zephaniah reminds readers that even high religious responsibilities do not guarantee safety in the face of the consequences of God's judgment on a rebellious nation. His role with the king and the prophet shows that some among the leaders of worship remained aware of the spiritual crisis, but this was not enough to save the kingdom or his own life.

sens: prophet of Judah in the 7th century B.C., son of Cushi
H6846H.detail: Zephaniah is a prophet sent by God to Judah during the reign of King Josiah (around 640-609 B.C.). His name means "the Lord has treasured" or "the Lord hides." He is a descendant of King Hezekiah and belongs to a priestly family. The book of Zephaniah contains his prophecies addressed to the people of Judah, announcing divine judgment on the kingdom and the surrounding nations, but also the hope of restoration for the humble and the righteous (Zephaniah 1:1).
H6846H.origine: The Hebrew name צְפַנְיָהוּ (Tsfanyahou) means "Yah has hidden" or "Yah has treasured," composed of the root צפן (tsafan, "to hide, to reserve") and the name of God יה (Yah). This name expresses the confidence that God protects or shelters His people. Zephaniah appears as the ninth minor prophet in the order of the biblical books.
H6846H.emploi: Zephaniah is mentioned only once in the Old Testament at Zephaniah 1:1, where he is presented with his complete genealogy: son of Cushi, grandson of Gedaliah, great-grandson of Amariah, and great-great-grandson of King Hezekiah. What makes Zephaniah unique is that unlike many other prophets, his genealogy is preserved in detail and traces back to a king. The book of Zephaniah, composed of three chapters, contains his prophetic words addressed to Judah during the reign of King Josiah, a time of religious reforms but also of external threat from Assyria.
H6846H.portee: The prophet Zephaniah reminds readers that before and after judgment, God remains attentive to His people, keeping and protecting them. His message emphasizes the importance of seeking justice and humility, and the promise that God always preserves a faithful remnant. For the Christian, Zephaniah shows how God can use a prophet to call His people to repentance and hope, even in times of crisis.

sens: man contemporary with the exile and return
father of Josiah and Hen
man whose name means "the Lord has reserved"
H6846I.detail: Zephaniah is a proper name designating a man living at the time of the exile and return from Babylon. He is mentioned as the father of Josiah and Hen, two men who receive special honor at the temple: their names are engraved on crowns kept as a memorial in the house of the Lord (Zechariah 6:14). Zephaniah appears as a witness or close to the captives returned from Babylon (Zechariah 6:10).
H6846I.origine: The name Zephaniah comes from Hebrew and literally means "the Lord has reserved" or "the Lord has treasured." This meaning reflects a trust in divine protection and providence, as if God carefully kept His people. It is a theophoric name, meaning it incorporates the divine name (Yah, abbreviation of the Lord).
H6846I.emploi: Zephaniah is mentioned twice in the book of Zechariah, in chapter 6. He appears only in this historical context of the return of the exiles from Babylon, under the reign of Darius and during the time of the prophet Zechariah. He is presented as the father of Josiah and Hen, two characters who receive public honor: crowns are made in their honor and kept as a memorial in the temple of the Lord. These mentions place him among the notable families of the people returned to Judah.

sens: Levite during the divided monarchy, son of Tahath
priest of the second order during the time of King Zedekiah, temple officer
H6846J.detail:
1. Zephaniah is first a Levite mentioned in the genealogy of the temple singers (1 Chronicles 6:36), son of Tahath and father of Uzziah. He lived during the time of the divided monarchy of Israel and Judah.
2. The name Zephaniah also designates a second-rank priest who served under King Zedekiah of Judah. This man was a temple officer and succeeded Jehoiada. He was killed at Riblah during the capture of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar.
H6846J.origine: The name Zephaniah comes from Hebrew and literally means "Jehovah has treasured" or "Jehovah has hidden." It combines two elements: the divine Name and the idea of preserving, reserving. This name expresses the action of God who keeps His people safe.
H6846J.emploi: The name Zephaniah appears in the Levitical genealogies of 1 Chronicles. The usage provided situates him in the lineage of Elkanah, at the heart of the lineage of the temple musicians. Although only one reference is given here, biblical tradition mentions several bearers of this name in the history of Israel, including priests and Levites who served in the temple worship.

sens: Egyptian name given to Joseph by Pharaoh
Honorific title meaning 'treasure of the glorious life' or 'the one who saves'
H6847.detail:
1. Tsaphnath-Paenéach is the Egyptian name that Pharaoh confers upon Joseph after elevating him to the rank of vizier (Genesis 41:45). This new name marks his entry into Egyptian life and his new authority: he is no longer the Hebrew slave, but Pharaoh's trusted man, responsible for administering the kingdom's resources.

2. The name literally means 'treasure of the glorious life' (or according to some, 'the one who saves'). It expresses both the dignity that Joseph acquires and his mission: to manage the grain during the famine, thus becoming the savior of Egypt and his own family.
H6847.origine: Tsaphnath-Paenéach is an Egyptian name, formed from words of ancient pharaonic vocabulary. Its exact etymology remains debated, but scholars see it as a composition meaning 'treasure' or 'the one who saves' associated with 'life' or 'glory.' In Hebrew, Joseph retains his original name (Yoséph), which means 'God will increase'; Pharaoh gives him a second name to integrate him into the Egyptian court and mark him as a man clothed with authority.
H6847.emploi: Tsaphnath-Paenéach appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 41:45, at the precise moment when Pharaoh recognizes Joseph's wisdom and appoints him governor of Egypt. This double name (Joseph and Tsaphnath-Paenéach) symbolizes the extraordinary destiny of this man: taken into slavery, he becomes one of the most powerful men in Egypt. Pharaoh also gives him an Egyptian wife, Asenath, marking his complete integration into Egyptian life while remaining faithful to his Hebrew roots.
H6847.portee: The change of Joseph's name to Tsaphnath-Paenéach reminds the reader that God can elevate His own beyond all expectation: from captive to minister of Pharaoh. It is an encouragement for the believer who goes through injustice or humiliation: God does not forget him and can transform his situation into honor and a holy mission. This Egyptian name also shows how God works beyond visible boundaries, granting favor and wisdom even in foreign lands.

sens: venomous serpent of the Bible, reputed to be particularly dangerous and deadly
mythological or legendary creature, king of serpents
H6848A.detail:
1. The basilisk is a venomous snake feared in biblical antiquity, likely a viper or a venomous snake that causes death through its venom. Although the Hebrew word primarily refers to this real reptile, the text of Isaiah imbues it with a superhuman dimension: it emerges from the root of the original serpent and begets a flying dragon, elevating it to the rank of a supernatural creature symbolizing divine threat and destruction against God's enemies.
2. In mythology and ancient literature, the basilisk became the 'king of serpents,' endowed with magical or superhuman powers. The Segond translates the Hebrew word with this mythical term to suggest that the text speaks of a creature more than ordinary, an instrument of divine punishment.
H6848A.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root צפע which describes a snake, probably a viper or a venomous reptile identified in ancient Levant. The Segond rendered it as 'basilisk,' the Greek name of the legendary king of serpents, to convey the idea of extreme danger and supernatural power associated with the prophetic text.
H6848A.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 14:29. The prophetic context is crucial: the prophet addresses the Philistines, announcing that a greater plague awaits them. From the root of the slain serpent will emerge a basilisk, and from it a flying dragon. This is an image of escalated threat and divine punishment: danger does not disappear with victory; it transforms into something even more terrible, escaping human control.
H6848A.portee: This passage teaches us that the enemy of God can never simply 'win': God has the final word, and His plans unfold even from what was believed to be destroyed. For the believer, this invites spiritual vigilance: a seemingly defeated threat can transform into a more pernicious form; only God's protection guarantees lasting victory.

sens: venomous reptile resembling a snake, particularly feared for its deadly venom
creature of the desert or wild places, symbol of danger and death
image of evil and divine destruction in the prophets
H6848B.detail:
1. The basilisk is a venomous reptile, probably a viper or another highly toxic snake (Isaiah 11:8 names it alongside the viper in the same den). Its venom kills anyone who eats its eggs (Isaiah 59:5), and its bite is deadly.
2. A creature dwelling in the lairs and caves of the desert or wild places, the basilisk symbolizes a danger that hides and strikes without warning: wine intoxicates as the basilisk stings (Proverbs 23:32).
3. In the mouths of the prophets, the basilisk becomes a weapon of divine judgment: the Lord sends these snakes to punish (Jeremiah 8:17), and the enemy 'hatches' basilisk eggs, an image of the evil plan that secretly germinates (Isaiah 59:5).
H6848B.origine: The Hebrew word צִפְעוֹנִי (tsiphoni) comes from the root צפע (tsapha), which designates the venomous snake in general. It is a concrete word that names a real creature from the ancient Near East. The Segond renders it as 'basilisk,' referencing a legendary creature feared in antiquity for its deadly venom, although it likely refers to a species of viper or cobra.
H6848B.emploi: This word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts of danger or judgment. In Proverbs 23:32, it describes the destructive effects of wine that intoxicates. Isaiah uses it twice: in 11:8, it announces an era of peace where the child can touch the basilisk's den without danger (messianic vision); in 59:5, it condemns those who 'hatch basilisk eggs,' an image of evil plans. Jeremiah 8:17 presents it as an instrument of the Lord's judgment against an unfaithful people. Each time, it evokes threat, death, and destructive power.
H6848B.portee: The basilisk teaches the reader that evil has real and deadly power, but faith in God protects against it. Isaiah 11:8 especially promises that in the time of salvation, the child (an image of vulnerability) will be saved from what terrified humanity. It is an invitation to trust despite the visible and invisible dangers of the world.

sens: shoot or branch that comes from a plant, tree, or root
figuratively, son or descendant of a family
H6849.detail:
1. The word literally refers to a young shoot or branch that grows on a plant or emerges from a root — the image of natural and living growth. In Isaiah 22:24, the prophet speaks of the 'noble and ignoble shoots' of the father's house, to evoke all descendants, both those of high rank and those of more modest condition.
2. Figuratively, the shoot represents a son or family member, someone who descends from it. This is how the Bible uses this word to speak of children or generations that extend the lineage of a house.
H6849.origine: The Hebrew word צְפִיעָה comes from a root that evokes the idea of pushing or springing forth. Its exact etymology remains uncertain, but the central image is that of a young branch that emerges from a trunk or mother plant — a natural image to speak of what is born and added to a stock. This image of organic growth easily applies to the descendants of a family.
H6849.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 22:24. The prophet describes the house of a father of a family and all those who depend on it — the children, the servants, the utensils. He speaks of the 'noble and ignoble shoots,' which means all descendants, from the most honorable to the most humble. The context shows that the shoot is one who belongs to a lineage and perpetuates the name and fortune. The adjective 'ignoble' (or 'despised') indicates that some shoots may have less importance or honor than others within the house.
H6849.portee: This word reminds us that every child, every descendant of a family is a precious shoot, a new life arising from a lineage. Even if some are less honored than others in the eyes of men, the Bible recognizes that all members of a house — from the most noble to the most humble — are connected by a living and organic bond. It is a beautiful image for understanding the importance of family and transmission.

sens: to emit high and light sounds, like a bird would
to produce a faint and indistinct murmur
H6850.detail: 1. The word primarily describes the small cries of birds: chirps, tweets, high and repeated sounds. In Isaiah 10:14, the prophet mentions birds that do not flap their wings or open their beaks to 'make' a sound — it is the image of the animal's natural cry. 2. Figuratively, it describes human sounds that imitate this chirping: faint murmurs, whispers, almost moans. In Isaiah 8:19, the 'whistling' refers to mediums who consult the dead — mysterious and unsettling sounds. In Isaiah 29:4, the voice of the humiliated people 'murmurs' from the dust like that of a specter. In Isaiah 38:14, the sick person cries out like a swallows fluttering, with faint and plaintive moans.
H6850.origine: The Hebrew word carries the idea of a small and repeated sound. It belongs to a family of imitative words that reproduce natural noises. Its basic image is that of a bird's chirping, a high and discontinuous sound that can be compared to whistling. This onomatopoeia evokes something small, light, contrasting with loud cries or clear words.
H6850.emploi: This verb appears four times in the Bible, all in Isaiah. It is used to describe the sounds of animals (birds) and faint or mysterious human sounds. Isaiah 8:19 uses it for the 'whistling' of mediums who claim to speak to the dead — these strange and hollow noises characterize their occult practices. Isaiah 10:14 refers to the cry that birds might emit. Isaiah 29:4 and 38:14 apply the word to human moans: the devastated people murmuring like a ghost, or the sick person crying plaintively. Each time, the word refers to faint, indistinct, or unsettling sounds.
H6850.portee: This word reminds us that God's people should not seek their answers from the dead or spirits — these sources produce only mysterious and empty 'whistlings.' In the face of anxiety or humiliation, our cry, even if faint, should rise to the Lord rather than to the occult powers that produce only hollow murmurs.

sens: Tree with flexible branches and narrow leaves, that grows near water
H6851.detail: 1. The willow is a tree of wet regions, recognizable by its supple and slender branches, and its elongated leaves. In Ezekiel 17:5, the eagle plants it 'near abundant water,' which shows that this tree needs moisture and proximity to water to grow. The Hebrews were well acquainted with it, as it abounds near the Jordan and water sources in the Holy Land.
H6851.origine: The Hebrew word צַפְצָפָה (tsaph.tsa.phah) literally designates the willow by the image of its branches swaying and oscillating (the root evokes this characteristic flexibility). This term names the tree directly by its most remarkable nature: its great suppleness and ability to bend without breaking, making it a useful tree for work and a symbol of plasticity.
H6851.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (Ezekiel 17:5). In this prophetic vision, the eagle plants a willow in fertile soil near abundant waters, symbolizing the planting of King Zedekiah in Babylon under King Nebuchadnezzar's rule. The choice of the willow is telling: it is a tree that needs water to live, an image of dependence and fragility in relation to the one who plants it.
H6851.portee: The willow reminds us that our spiritual growth needs to be close to God, just as the willow needs water. It is also an image of humility and flexibility: the willow does not resist storms; it bends. For the believer, this is a lesson on the importance of staying near the living source (God) and not becoming rigid in pride.

sens: to leave, to go away early in the morning
to retreat, to withdraw from a trial or commitment
H6852.detail:
1. The verb first evokes the idea of leaving early, getting up early to set out — a material and concrete action: leaving a place at dawn.
2. In the context of Judges 7:3, where Gideon cries, 'Let whoever is fearful and afraid withdraw from Mount Gilead,' the meaning shifts toward retreat, withdrawal. Those who 'withdraw' are not merely early travelers: they are soldiers who are afraid and retreating from battle. The word thus expresses the action of stepping away, removing oneself from a difficult or threatening situation.
H6852.origine: The Hebrew root צפר (tsafar) is rarely attested in the Old Testament. Its primary etymology likely refers to dawn, early morning (root צפ), and thus to the natural action of leaving early. The meaning has extended to any form of departure or retreat. The context of fear in Judges 7:3 shows how the word can denote a flight that is not voluntary and enthusiastic, but motivated by fear.
H6852.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Judges 7:3, in the account where Gideon asks his fearful soldiers to leave the battlefield. This unique occurrence shows withdrawal as an act of retreat in the face of danger. The military context and the call for courage from the remaining soldiers (who will then undergo Yahweh's test) make this verb associated with weakness, fear that paralyzes and leads to abandonment.
H6852.portee: This word reminds us that fear easily leads to retreat and abandonment. But Gideon's account also shows that God prefers a small army of brave hearts to a crowd of fearful soldiers: those who remain will be led to a miraculous victory by God Himself, not by their number or strength.

sens: winged creature that flies in the sky
living creature that feeds and shelters in trees
figuratively: lightness or fragility
H6853.detail:
1. The bird is a winged creature capable of flight. It is the quintessential animal of the sky, one that moves freely in the air. In Nebuchadnezzar's vision in Daniel 4:12, the birds of the sky make their home in the branches of the giant tree, symbolizing the king's greatness.
2. The bird is a living being that depends on nature's resources to survive: it feeds, seeks shelter, and a place to dwell. In Daniel 4:14, when the king orders the tree to be cut down, the birds that have made their nests there must also be scattered, showing that this tree was both refuge and source of food for them.
3. The word also evokes fragility and lightness: Nebuchadnezzar's hair and nails grow 'like the feathers of eagles' (Daniel 4:33), an image of degradation and dehumanization, where what constituted his royal dignity becomes as light and simple as the plumage of a beast.
H6853.origine: The Aramaic word צְפַר (tsepar) is related to the Hebrew word צִפּוֹר (tsippor), both stemming from a root that evokes the chirping or singing of birds. These words reflect a world where the bird was such a common and visible creature that its presence was heard before it was seen. The same Hebrew word appears in many ancient biblical texts.
H6853.emploi: This word appears only four times in Daniel 4, all in the account of King Nebuchadnezzar's dream where he sees a great cosmic tree. The first three occurrences (verses 12, 14, and 21) use it to describe the birds of the sky that find refuge and nourishment in this wonderful tree, showing the abundance and prosperity of this royal symbol. The fourth occurrence (verse 33) uses it in an image of degradation: the king's hair becomes 'like the feathers of eagles,' marking his bestial transformation as divine punishment. The term remains always concrete, without moral connotation, but in this visionary context, it carries a strong symbolic charge.
H6853.portee: This account reminds the reader that even the most powerful of kings is a creature subject to God. The birds, free and carefree, contrast with the humiliating fall of Nebuchadnezzar reduced to an animal state. The text teaches that pride leads to destruction and that only one who recognizes divine sovereignty can be restored.

sens: Small aquatic animal with smooth skin that jumps and croaks
Creature sent by God as punishment upon Egypt
H6854.detail:
1. The frog is an animal that lives in water and on land, known for its jumps and croaks. It is a common amphibian in Egypt, particularly in the Nile and marshes.
2. In the account of the plagues of Egypt, frogs become an instrument of God's judgment: they invaded the land, climbed on people, entered houses, courtyards, and fields until they covered the entire territory (Exodus 8:2). This supernatural multiplication of frogs demonstrates divine power and forces Pharaoh to acknowledge that he must let the people of Israel go (Exodus 8:4).
H6854.origine: The Hebrew word צְפַרְדֵּעַ (tsephardéa) likely evokes the sound made by the frog. It appears only in the accounts of the plagues of Egypt and in the psalms that remember them. It is a rare term, limited to these specific contexts where it carries a theological weight: the frog becomes a symbol of God's omnipotence over creation and divine judgment.
H6854.emploi: The word appears 13 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the account of the ten plagues of Egypt (Exodus 7:27 to 8:9). It recounts how, at the word of Moses and under the power of the Lord, frogs covered Egypt, causing a terrifying plague: they invaded homes, multiplied everywhere, and forced Pharaoh to beg Moses to make them disappear (Exodus 8:4 and 8:7). This plague demonstrates that the gods of Egypt are powerless. It is also recalled in the Psalms (78:45 and 105:30) as a memorable act of the Lord's power and faithfulness to His people.
H6854.portee: This plague of frogs reveals how God uses even the most ordinary creatures to accomplish His purpose and demonstrate His supremacy. It invites the reader to recognize that nothing escapes the control of the God of Israel, and that He can transform nature to free His oppressed people. It is a narrative that affirms the freedom and power of God in the face of false gods and human powers.

sens: Wife of Moses and daughter of Jethro
Mother of Gershom and Eliezer
H6855.detail:
1. Zipporah is the wife of Moses. She is the daughter of Jethro, a Midianite priest who welcomed Moses when he fled Egypt. Moses marries her and stays with her father (Exodus 2:21). She accompanies him on his return to Egypt and during the events in the desert.

2. Zipporah is the mother of two sons: Gershom and Eliezer. Her maternal role is particularly evident at the crossing of the Red Sea, when she performs the radical act of circumcising her son with a sharp stone (Exodus 4:25), thus saving her husband from divine judgment. She embodies a woman of courage and faith at the critical moment of Israel's deliverance.
H6855.origine: The name Zipporah means "bird" in Hebrew, derived from the root צִפֹּר (tsippor). It is a simple and poetic name suitable for a young woman from the family of Jethro, priest of Midian. The name reflects Semitic culture where animal names were often used to describe qualities: lightness, agility, speed.
H6855.emploi: Zipporah appears only three times in the Bible, all in the book of Exodus. First, she is introduced as the wife that Moses takes from Jethro (Exodus 2:21). Then, she plays a dramatic role by circumcising her son during the night, likely to appease God's anger towards Moses (Exodus 4:25). Finally, she is mentioned when she returns to Moses after being temporarily separated from him (Exodus 18:2). Through these brief passages, she appears as a woman submitted to God and ready to act with determination at decisive moments.
H6855.portee: Zipporah shows that women play an indispensable role in the history of salvation, even when they remain in the background. Her act of circumcision in Exodus 4:25 reveals her faith: she understands the importance of God's covenant and acts without hesitation to protect her husband and children. She reminds the reader that faithfulness to God does not always require spectacular gestures, but daily obedience and courage in times of need.

sens: The hard, keratinous tip that covers the ends of fingers and toes
The sharp point of a tool or hard stone capable of engraving
H6856.detail:
1. The nail is the hard part that grows at the tip of our fingers: in Deuteronomy 21:12, a captive woman "will make her nails," meaning she will cut or maintain them, as a gesture of hygiene and personal care during a period of mourning. This is the most common meaning of the word.
2. By extension, the word also refers to the fine, sharp point of a tool or gem: in Jeremiah 17:1, the prophet speaks of a "point of diamond" that engraves the sin of Judah on the stone — a powerful image of the stylus or needle that digs and marks indelibly. The nail, like the point of the diamond, is something small yet fearfully incisive.
H6856.origine: The Hebrew word צִפֹּרֶן comes from a root that evokes the idea of "pointing" or "stabbing." In Aramaic, the word טְפַר means "nail" or "claw." These words from the same family emphasize the sharp and piercing nature, whether referring to the nail of the body or the point of a cutting instrument. The basic image is of something small, hard, and capable of marking or wounding.
H6856.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, making it a rather rare term. In Deuteronomy 21:12, it literally refers to the human nail in a context of grooming and personal hygiene — it is a detail of the law concerning captive women. In Jeremiah 17:1, the meaning takes on symbolic weight: the "point" of the diamond becomes a metaphor for the stylus or chisel that engraves and marks permanently. These two uses show how the same word can shift from the concrete (the part of the body) to the figurative (the instrument that engraves), both retaining the idea of something sharp and penetrating.
H6856.portee: The word reminds us that even the smallest details of our lives — our acts of care, our hygiene — have a place in God's word. But above all, the image of the diamond point that engraves challenges us: sin, once inscribed in the heart through habit or hardness, leaves a deep and almost indelible mark. This calls for vigilance and sincere repentance.

sens: City of Canaan inhabited by the Canaanites, located in the territory of Simeon
H6857.detail: Tsephath is a city in Canaan that was occupied by the Canaanites before the Israelite conquest. Its name means "watchtower" or "place of observation." After the victory of the Israelites Judah and Simeon against its inhabitants, the city was destroyed by the ban (devoted to the Lord by destruction) and received the new name Hormah, which means "destruction" or "devastation" (Judges 1:17).
H6857.origine: The name Tsephath comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of watching, observing, or surveilling from a high point — hence "watchtower." It was a Canaanite name that the Israelites replaced with Hormah after the conquest, a common name change in the Bible to mark the transition of a place under Israelite control.
H6857.emploi: Tsephath appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 1:17. It is mentioned as one of the Canaanite cities conquered during the entry into the Promised Land. The tribes of Judah and Simeon attacked it together, defeated its Canaanite inhabitants, and completely destroyed the city by devoting it to the Lord. This raid is part of the early battles of the period of the Judges.

sens: Architectural element placed at the top of a column or pillar
Ornate crown of a column
Decorated part that connects the shaft of a column to its supporting base
H6858.detail:
1. The capital is the architectural piece that crowns the top of a column or pillar. It serves as a transitional element between the shaft (the cylindrical body) and what rests on top. In the temple of Jerusalem that Solomon built, the two large bronze columns at the entrance had capitals of five cubits (approximately 2.5 meters) in height, carefully crafted and adorned (2 Chronicles 3:15).
2. The capital can be clad, meaning covered with plates of bronze or other precious metal, giving the column a rich and majestic appearance. This ornamentation made it a visible and remarkable element of the building, far beyond its simple function of support.
H6858.origine: The Hebrew word צֶפֶת likely comes from a root related to cutting or hollow shape. It literally designates something rounded or curved that overhangs. The capitals of Solomon's temple were inspired by architectural styles of the ancient Near East, where such crowns were essential to the decor and visual balance of monumental constructions.
H6858.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 3:15, during the detailed description of the temple that Solomon built in Jerusalem. The text emphasizes the impressive dimensions of the columns and the beauty of their capitals, highlighting the luxury and perfection of the building dedicated to God. The context shows that the capital was much more than a simple technical element: it was a centerpiece of the ornamentation of the sanctuary.
H6858.portee: The capital of the temple reminds us that God's house was built with care and magnificence, reflecting divine glory. For the reader, this architectural detail illustrates how every part of the temple, even the most visible, was designed to express the holiness and majesty of God. It invites us to consider how we honor God through the care we give to what is dedicated to Him.

sens: City in the south of Judah, later allotted to Simeon
Residence of David when he fled from Saul
Rallying center for David's warriors
H6860.detail:
1. Ziklag is a city located in the southern territory of Judah, mentioned as early as the division of the lands among the tribes after the conquest (Joshua 15:31). It was later assigned to the tribe of Simeon. It is a strategic location in this desert region of the Negev.

2. King Achish of Gath granted Ziklag to David when he was fleeing from King Saul and seeking refuge among the Philistines (1 Samuel 27:6). David established his residence there and stayed during his years of flight, away from the territory controlled by Saul.

3. Ziklag became the rallying point for many mighty warriors who came to join David. Thus, men from Manasseh joined him at Ziklag when he returned to the city (1 Chronicles 12:20). It is also where David learned of Saul's death (2 Samuel 1:1), marking a decisive turning point in his story.
H6860.origine: The name Ziklag literally means "twisting" or "winding," probably referring to the rugged terrain and winding paths of this region of the Negev. The geographical site shaped the name of the place.
H6860.emploi: Ziklag appears 12 times in the Bible, mostly in the books of Samuel and Chronicles. It is first mentioned among the cities of southern Judah (Joshua 15:31). It is primarily as David's refuge that it becomes significant: King Achish grants it to him, and David gathers his troops there before becoming king of Israel. After Saul's death, David receives the news of this event there (2 Samuel 1:1), confirming that Ziklag was his operational center during his flight. Even after his establishment in Jerusalem, the city remains associated with King David and the Judean monarchy (1 Samuel 27:6).
H6860.portee: Ziklag symbolizes divine providence in trials. While David was pursued and without a safe refuge, God prepared a city for him where he could hide and where his faithful could gather. It is the place where the community of David's warriors is forged, foreshadowing his future reign. For the believer, Ziklag reminds us that even in times of crisis and flight, God prepares a place of refuge and strength.

sens: Container or envelope used to hold and transport goods
Bag made of fabric or skin intended to carry grain, bread, agricultural products
H6861.detail:
1. The word designates a container, usually made of fabric or skin, used for transporting items. In the only biblical usage we know, a man brings "new ears of grain in his sack" to Elisha (2 Kings 4:42): it is an ordinary container for carrying harvests or foodstuffs.
2. It is a type of pouch or transport bag, used in the daily life of farmers and travelers to convey products and provisions. The image is one of agricultural work and simple exchanges in the ancient Near East.
H6861.origine: The Hebrew word tsiqlon has an uncertain etymology and its original image remains obscure. It belongs to the simple and concrete vocabulary of agricultural life. The term appears only once in the Bible, making its history difficult to trace: it is a rare word, perhaps limited to a specific region or time in Hebrew speech.
H6861.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 4:42. An inhabitant of Baal-Shalisha brings to Elisha bread and new ears of grain contained in this sack. The context is that of offering to the prophets: it is a gesture of respect towards the man of God. The sack is simply the ordinary object that allows for the transport of the gifts of the harvest.
H6861.portee: This small detail in the biblical text reminds us of the simple and concrete life of the Hebrew people: goods were brought on foot, in ordinary containers. It also shows how the Israelites honored the prophets by offering them the products of their labor and land, a gesture of trust and submission to the word of God.

sens: Having little space, little width
That oppresses, that tightens, that constricts
Adversary, enemy that presses or attacks
Tightly together, united in a compact manner
H6862A.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: a narrow place is one where space is lacking, where one cannot expand. In 2 Kings 6:1, the sons of the prophets tell Elisha that their dwelling is "too narrow" for them — they lack space to live together. Similarly, in Isaiah 49:20, Jerusalem complains that "the space is too narrow" to accommodate all its returning inhabitants.
2. The word also evokes the idea of something that constricts, presses, or confines like a vise. A "narrow" well (Proverbs 23:27) is not just small: it is a place from which one cannot escape, a prison.
3. By a beautiful extension, "narrow" comes to designate one who constricts, who oppresses: the adversary or enemy. In 1 Samuel 2:32, God speaks to Eli about an "adversary" who will arise in his house — this is a figurative sense, where the word describes one who constricts you, who threatens you.
4. Applied to objects, the word expresses the idea of things tightly together. In Job 41:6, the mighty shields of Leviathan are "united" together as if by a seal — so tightly that they cannot be separated.
H6862A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew-Aramaic root that fundamentally means "to press," "to squeeze." The starting image is tactile: something that presses, that constricts. From there comes the concrete sense of "narrow" (that which constricts space), then the figurative sense of "adversary" (one who constricts you, who oppresses) or "enemy" (one who tightens around you). Words of the same family express the idea of distress, anguish — the state of one who is pressed on all sides.
H6862A.emploi: This word appears 8 times in the provided texts, primarily in two usages. First, in the concrete sense of "narrow": a space that is too small (2 Kings 6:1, Isaiah 49:20), a well from which one cannot escape (Proverbs 23:27). Secondly, in the figurative sense of "adversary" or "enemy": in 1 Samuel 2:32, it is the enemy who oppresses Eli's house. The passage from Job 41:6 shows the word applied to things: the "united" shields of Leviathan. Throughout all these uses, we see how the word retains the basic idea: something or someone that constricts, that oppresses, that leaves no space.
H6862A.portee: This word helps us understand how the Bible speaks of difficulties and enemies: not as abstractions, but as realities that "constrict," that "press," that take up space in our lives. When the Bible says that a place or situation is "narrow," it evokes a concrete oppression. When it calls the adversary "narrow," it describes him as one who constricts you, who threatens you. It is an image to remind us that difficulties and enemies affect our living space and our freedom.

sens: State of intense suffering, oppression, or danger
Critical moment when everything seems impossible
Desperate call addressed to God
H6862B.detail:
1. Distress is primarily a situation of tightening, of compression: it constricts the one who experiences it. It is the experience of being caught in a vise, with no escape. When David declares, "I am in great distress" (1 Chronicles 21:13), he describes this weight that crushes, this oppression of the heart in the face of inevitable judgment.
2. It is also the extremity, the moment when human resources are exhausted. The psalmists cry out, "In their distress, they cried out to the Lord" (Psalms 107:28): it is when everything seems lost that prayer bursts forth. Nothing can help except God Himself.
3. Distress thus becomes the occasion for supplication, the cry of one who has no hope of help except from the Lord. "For them my lips have opened, and my mouth has spoken in my distress" (Psalms 66:14): suffering becomes prayer.
H6862B.origine: The Hebrew word צַר (tsar) literally means "narrow, constricted." It comes from a root that expresses the idea of compression and strangulation. That is why it describes both a narrow passage and a situation that suffocates the soul. The same word can designate an adversary, one who constricts, who oppresses. In biblical language, the physical and the spiritual are linked: a narrow street becomes the image of anguish that tightens the throat and heart.
H6862B.emploi: The word appears 31 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Psalms and the book of Job, where men in suffering cry out to God. It designates either a situation of military or political danger (Judges 11:7, Isaiah 25:4) or personal and spiritual tribulation. Distress is often the starting point of prayer: men plead with the Lord to be delivered from it. In the lament psalms (like Psalm 107), this word recurs as a refrain to show how God hears the cry of the unfortunate. It can also be a pedagogical trial, which God allows to test faith (Deuteronomy 4:30, Isaiah 30:20).
H6862B.portee: Distress is never presented as definitive in the Bible. It is the path that leads to God: it is in anguish that one learns to pray sincerely, to renounce false recourses. For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that suffering can be the school of faith, and that the Lord is closer in times of constriction than anywhere else.

sens: one who fought against Israel on the battlefield or waged war against it
one who opposes someone with hostility or malice
one who oppresses or exercises cruel domination
one who threatens or seeks to harm peace
figure of evil or that which opposes God
H6862C.detail: 1. The word primarily designates a military adversary, one who is confronted in war: Abram praises God who delivered his enemies into his hands (Genesis 14:20), a classic image of victory in battle. 2. Beyond war, it refers to one who harbors hostility, threatens, or seeks to do harm: the enemies of Judah and Benjamin opposed the rebuilding of the temple (Ezra 4:1), and the psalmist prays to God not to deliver him to the will of his adversaries (Psalms 27:12). 3. The enemy can also be the oppressor, one who exercises tyrannical domination: the psalmist sings of how God delivered them from their oppressors (Psalms 136:24), and Jerusalem weeps under the hand of the oppressor (Lamentations 1:7). 4. The term extends to any threat against peace or salvation, particularly in hymns where God promises to crush adversaries (Psalms 89:24). 5. It also takes on a spiritual significance: the enemy becomes the figure of all that opposes God's plan and His people.
H6862C.origine: The Hebrew word צַר (tsar) comes from a root that evokes the idea of tightening, pressing, or constricting: the enemy is one who tightens, who oppresses. This root can also mean "distress" or "tribulation," as the enemy is the source of distress. The same word carries several nuances—combatant, hostile opponent, oppressor—depending on the context, but always with the idea of hostile pressure or threat.
H6862C.emploi: The word צַר appears 66 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms, where it is very frequent. It primarily designates the military enemy in historical accounts (Genesis, Ezra, Nehemiah), then the adversary of the righteous in wisdom literature and laments. In the Psalms, it constantly recurs: the psalmist asks God to defeat or protect against his enemies (Psalms 27:2, 44:6-8, 89:24). The term is also used for the oppressor who crushes the people (Lamentations 1:7, Psalms 136:24). In the prophets, it can refer to the historical enemy (Jeremiah, Isaiah) or opposition to the divine plan. The usages show a gradation: from physical combat to spiritual hostility, from the particular (besieged Jerusalem) to the universal (that which opposes God).
H6862C.portee: This word reminds Christians that the Bible acknowledges the real existence of opposition and hostility—not out of pessimism, but to invite seeking protection in God. The Psalms teach that in the face of the enemy, one should not rely on oneself but on the strength of the Lord: "I do not trust in my bow, and my sword does not save me" (Psalms 44:7). This word invites abandoning fear and carnal vengeance to trust in God, who promises to crush the adversary and grant victory. It also challenges Christians regarding their own enemies: how to see them? how to treat them in light of the Gospel that commands love for enemies?

sens: hard and smooth stone, such as flint or pebble
hard and compact material, resistant to wear
figuratively: that which is inflexible, relentless
H6862D.detail:
1. The word designates a hard and compact stone, particularly flint or smooth pebble. In Isaiah 5:28, the hooves of war horses are compared to hard stones: this indicates their solidity and ability to strike the ground without wearing out, even at a gallop.
2. The image evokes hardness itself—what resists, does not yield, does not crumble. It is the raw, mineral material, opposed to what is soft or fragile.
3. Figuratively, this term can evoke moral hardness: something hard, relentless, that does not bend. But this figurative usage remains close to the concrete image in the biblical text.
H6862D.origine: The Hebrew word צַר (tsar) literally means "hard" or "tight." It comes from a root that expresses tension, rigidity, compaction. The word is related to the idea of what presses, what is narrow or constricted—hence the image of mineral hardness. This same root is found in other Hebrew words meaning "adversary" or "enemy," as the enemy is one who "tightens," who oppresses.
H6862D.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 5:28, where it describes the hooves of warrior horses. The prophet enumerates the formidable elements of the Assyrian army or an enemy power: sharp arrows, drawn bows, and these hard hooves like flint. The usage is highly concrete and poetic, serving to reinforce the image of irresistible military power and destruction advancing without obstacle.
H6862D.portee: This word reminds us that raw military power, as impressive as it may be, is merely dead matter—horses, weapons, metal. It contrasts with the power of God, who alone can stop this destructive march. For the believer, it is an invitation not to fear the strength of men, however hard it may seem.

sens: fortified city of Naphtali
H6863.detail: Tser is a fortified city located in the territory of the tribe of Naphtali, probably near the Sea of Galilee. It is listed in verse 35 of chapter 19 of Joshua among the cities that the Israelites received as an inheritance after the conquest of the land of Canaan.
H6863.origine: The name Tser likely comes from a root meaning "flint" or "hard stone," which could evoke the rocky nature of the terrain or a characteristic of the site. Although this place is mentioned only once in the Bible, its inclusion in the list of cities assigned to Naphtali shows that it had administrative and strategic importance.
H6863.emploi: Tser appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:35. It is included in the list of fortified cities that the tribe of Naphtali received as an inheritance after Israel conquered Canaan. This mention fits into the context of the division of territory among the twelve tribes. Its status as a "strong city" suggests that it was an important and defended center.

sens: hard and sharp stone, naturally pointed or shaped
rock or hard stone in a figurative sense, symbol of hardness and strength
H6864.detail: 1. Flint is a naturally hard and brittle stone from which very sharp edges could be obtained by striking. It was formerly used as a knife or razor for delicate operations. In Exodus 4:25, Zipporah takes a "sharp stone" of flint to perform a circumcision—it is the most suitable instrument for this precise task. 2. Figuratively, the hardness of flint becomes the image of immutable strength and tenacity. In Ezekiel 3:9, God compares the prophet's forehead to a diamond and to flint: it is a promise that nothing will make him bend in the face of the hostility of the rebellious people.
H6864.origine: The Hebrew word צֹר comes from a root that evokes hardness and resistance. Flint was well known in the ancient Near East: it is the most practical stone for obtaining a sharp blade without metal, hence its use in religious rites and daily tasks. It is also a very common mineral, used since prehistoric times.
H6864.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible. In both cases, it designates extreme hardness: first as a surgical instrument of rare precision (Exodus 4:25), then as a symbol of unwavering moral resistance (Ezekiel 3:9). The context changes but the idea remains: flint embodies what is hard, precise, impossible to break.
H6864.portee: This word reminds the believer that God equips His people—and particularly His prophets—with a strength comparable to flint: impervious to pressure, incapable of bending under attacks. It also invites recognizing that God provides for our needs, even the most precise, with the right means.

sens: Phoenician coastal city on the Mediterranean
Major commercial center and maritime power in antiquity
Symbol of human wealth and pride in the face of God
H6865.detail:
1. Tyre is a fortified city built on a rock on the Mediterranean coast (its name means "rock"), located north of Israel in present-day Phoenician territory. It is mentioned as early as the time of the kings of Israel when Hiram, its king, sends wood and workers for the construction of the temple (2 Samuel 5:11, 1 Kings 5:1).

2. Tyre was famous for its maritime trade, ships, and wealth. Ezekiel describes it as a prosperous economic power, trading with many peoples (Ezekiel 27). The city was one of the most influential on the Phoenician coast alongside Sidon.

3. In prophecies, Tyre represents human pride and opposition to God. Ezekiel 28:2 shows its prince declaring, "I am God," which brings divine judgment. God announces its destruction by Nebuchadnezzar (Ezekiel 26:7), symbolizing the punishment of those who rise against the Lord.
H6865.origine: The Hebrew name צֹר (Tsor) literally means "rock," reflecting the natural geography of the city built on a rocky island. This name describes the location rather than designating it by an ordinary term, which was common in ancient Near Eastern fortified cities.
H6865.emploi: Tyre is mentioned 39 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the historical books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) and prophetic books (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Isaiah). In the time of David and Solomon, Tyre was an established trading partner: Hiram provides cedar wood and craftsmen for the temple (2 Samuel 5:11, 1 Kings 5:1). The prophets, especially Ezekiel (chapters 26-28), pronounce oracles of judgment against it for its pride, its wicked trade, and its alliances contrary to God's plans. Ezekiel 27 composes a lamentation over its wealth and downfall. Psalm 87:4 includes it among the peoples called to know God. Isaiah 23 also announces its humiliation. Joel and Amos mention it for its relations with Israel and Judah.
H6865.portee: Tyre teaches that material prosperity and worldly prestige do not protect against divine justice. Its pride—claiming to be a god or equaling God—leads to its ruin. For the believer, Tyre is a historical example of the vanity of earthly riches and the importance of humility before the Lord. It also shows that God governs the history of all nations, even those that ignore or reject Him.

sens: To be affected by fire and intense heat
To be consumed or dried up by heat
H6866.detail:
1. The word describes the action of fire on an object: to be burned is to undergo the destructive action of flame and heat. In Ezekiel 21:3, the fire of the Lord ignites the forest of the south, and every face will be burned: this is the image of total destruction by fire, which consumes both green and dry trees, and even reaches living creatures.
2. By extension, the verb can evoke the drying up or profound alteration caused by extreme heat—not only visible destruction but also the devastating and irreversible effect of fire.
H6866.origine: The root צרב (tsa.rav) expresses the idea of burning and consuming. The Hebrew verb primarily evokes the physical action of fire on matter. The niphal form (passive voice) used here shows not the action of burning something, but the fact of being burned, of passively undergoing the destructive effect of the flame. This type of construction emphasizes the power of the agent that burns (here, divine fire) and the vulnerability of what is affected.
H6866.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 21:3. The context is an oracle of judgment: the Lord announces that He will ignite a destructive fire in the forest of the south, and this fire will burn all faces. The term fits into a threatening prophecy addressed to earthly kingdoms, where divine fire symbolizes inevitable judgment. Its uniqueness in usage makes it a rare word, but its meaning is clear in this dramatic context.
H6866.portee: This word reminds us of the reality of divine judgment: the fire of the Lord is not an empty threat, but a real and destructive power that consumes all that opposes His will. For the Christian reader, this illustrates the holiness of God and the impossibility of escaping His judgment without repentance. The burning fire becomes a striking image of the gravity of sin and the necessity of turning to God before it is too late.

sens: That burns with intensity, that consumes
That is intense and destructive
H6867A.detail:
1. The word describes what burns with force and bright heat. In Proverbs 16:27, the words of a wicked man are compared to a "burning fire" on his lips: an image of words that burn, consume, and destroy like fire consumes wood.
2. Figuratively, the adjective characterizes what is intense, violent, and destructive in its effects. The burning words of the wicked ravage like a wildfire, deeply wounding those who listen to them.
H6867A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the action of burning and consuming. The basic image is that of fire that ravages and destroys. This root is found in several Hebrew words related to burning and the destructive heat it causes. The word belongs to the semantic family of fire and the destruction it provokes.
H6867A.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 16:27. It is a poetic image to describe the harmful words of a wicked or perverse man. The Bible often compares harmful words to a fire that destroys: here, the burning fire on the lips symbolizes the destructive power of slander, calumny, or lies spoken with malicious intent.
H6867A.portee: This verse teaches the reader that words are not trivial: they can burn, wound, and destroy like real fire. Those who fear God must watch their words and reject malice, for the burning words of the wicked leave traces of destruction. This invites the Christian to restraint, kindness, and to weigh their words before speaking them.

sens: Persistent mark left by the healing of a wound or burn
Sign of closure and consolidation of a skin lesion
H6867B.detail:
1. A scar is the visible trace that remains after a wound or burn has healed. It is the tissue that reforms and covers the injury. In Leviticus 13:23, when the priest examines a person and sees that "it is a scar from the ulcer," he recognizes that the wound has closed and that the person can be declared clean — it is a good sign, the affliction has ceased to progress.
2. A scar indicates that the lesion is no longer spreading and poses no further danger. In Leviticus 13:28, a burn that "has become pale" and forms a scar shows that the healing process is underway and that ritual contamination is disappearing: the priest recognizes it as a scar and declares the person clean.
H6867B.origine: The Hebrew word צָרֶבֶת (tsarévet) comes from the root צרב (tsarab), which means "to burn." A scar is therefore literally what "remains of the burn" or damage. It is the tissue that persists after fire or injury has marked the skin. In biblical Hebrew, this word appears exclusively in the context of ritual purity examinations in Leviticus, where scars play a specific role: they mark the end of an active affliction and the beginning of healing.
H6867B.emploi: The word appears twice in the Bible, both in Leviticus 13, at the heart of the purity code concerning skin diseases. In these two verses, the priest must distinguish a scar — a sign of consolidation and cessation of the disease — from an affliction that is still active. When he sees a scar that has not progressed and whose color is changing (fading), he recognizes that the healing process has taken place and that the person can be declared ritually clean. The scar is therefore a positive marker of the favorable outcome of a skin disease.
H6867B.portee: For the reader, the scar reminds us that even after a serious injury or burn, healing is possible and visible. It is a sign that God allows the restoration of the body. In the Israelite ritual system, the scar does not render the person unclean: on the contrary, it proves that the affliction has ceased. This invites the believer to see in the scar not a shame or a stain, but the evidence of ongoing healing and a return to normalcy.

sens: City or territory of Manasseh in Northern Israel
H6868G.detail: Tseréda is a locality in the territory of Manasseh, in the northern kingdom of Israel. It is the birthplace of Jeroboam, the first king of Israel after the schism: he is described as an Ephraimite from Tseréda, son of Nebat and a widow (1 Kings 11:26). The name likely means "fortress," evoking a fortified or defended place.
H6868G.origine: The name literally means "fortress." Tseréda is a historical locality in the territory of Ephraim or Manasseh, in the northern region of Palestine. Its archaeological identification remains uncertain, but it was likely a well-known city or town at the time of the writing of the account of Jeroboam.
H6868G.emploi: Tseréda appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 11:26. It is mentioned as the birthplace of Jeroboam, the servant of Solomon who was anointed king of Northern Israel (1 Kings 11:29-37). This geographical detail situates Jeroboam within the context of the Northern kingdom and anchors his story in a concrete and territorial Israel.

sens: Locality in the Jordan Valley, in Manasseh, near Succoth
H6868H.detail: Tseréda is a small town or region located in the Jordan plain, in the territory of Manasseh. It appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 4:17, where it is mentioned as one of the landmarks for locating the bronze castings made for Solomon's temple: "in a clay soil, between Succoth and Tseréda." It is a geographical place used to precisely identify where the metallurgical works of the king took place.
H6868H.origine: The name means "fortress" in Hebrew, evoking a fortified or defended place. Tseréda is also known by another biblical name, Zarethan (צָֽרְתָן), which designates the same place or a neighboring locality. This region of the Jordan was conducive to metal craftsmanship due to its clay soil and proximity to water.
H6868H.emploi: Tseréda appears only once in the transmitted biblical texts (2 Chronicles 4:17), where it serves as a geographical reference for locating Solomon's bronze casting workshops. It is mentioned alongside Succoth, another locality in the Jordan, confirming that it is an area known for its artisanal activities and its strategic importance in trade and metal fabrication.

sens: Extreme anguish, moment of great affliction
Situation of danger or imminent peril
Indigence, lack of necessities
State of abandonment or isolation in the face of trials
H6869A.detail:
1. Distress is primarily an intense inner state: anguish and moral suffering when one is overwhelmed by circumstances. In Psalms 9:10, the oppressed who cries out to the Lord does so "in the time of distress," that is, in his moment of greatest affliction.
2. It also designates an objective situation of danger or crisis: a peril that threatens and from which one sees no way out. The psalmist asks why God hides "in the time of distress" (Psalms 10:1), when the danger is most pressing.
3. The word also evokes lack, extreme poverty, indigence: one who lacks the necessities for life experiences material as well as moral distress.
4. By extension, it is the experience of being alone in the storm, without protection, without someone who could come to help — hence the psalmist's call to the Lord as refuge.
H6869A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes narrowness, confinement, what presses and suffocates. It is related to the word "tzar" (enemy, adversary), one who exerts pressure, constraint.
