The basic image is that of a vise: distress is a situation that constricts you, where you cannot breathe freely. This root is very ancient and widely attested in the Old Testament to describe critical moments for the people of Israel.
H6869A.emploi: This word appears only twice in the provided Psalms (Psalms 9:10 and 10:1), always at the moment when the psalmist cries out to God. It describes the existential context of prayer: it is precisely "in the time of distress" that the believer discovers that the Lord is his refuge. The word thus marks the contrast between the desperate human situation and divine intervention. Its use emphasizes that distress is the moment when faith in God takes on all its meaning and strength.
H6869A.portee: This word reminds the reader that distress is never the last word: it is, on the contrary, the moment when God reveals Himself as refuge. Knowing this word helps the Christian to name his experience of crisis and to understand that it can be a call to discover more deeply divine protection. It is an invitation to sincere prayer in the heart of the trial.

sens: State of anguish or physical suffering
Situation of immediate danger or peril
Calamity or misfortune affecting a people
Deep spiritual or moral crisis
State of urgent need addressed to God
H6869B.detail:
1. Distress is primarily the personal experience of suffering and anguish: it is the cry of the psalmist who says, "In my distress, I cry out to the Lord" (Psalms 120:1), or Jacob saying, "I will raise an altar to the God who answered me on the day of my distress" (Genesis 35:3).
2. It also refers to the straits of immediate danger, when one is trapped: the Israelites in Nehemiah 9:27 cry out to God "in the time of their distress" when their enemies oppress them, and the righteous find protection "in the time of distress" (Psalms 37:39).
3. It can be a collective calamity that strikes an entire people: Isaiah 8:22 paints a horizon of distress and darkness for a nation, and Jeremiah 30:7 speaks of Jacob's distress as a historical catastrophe.
4. On a spiritual level, it is also the moment of crisis where the soul is in deep turmoil, as in Psalms 77:3 where suffering even prevents rest.
5. Biblically, distress is always the moment when one cries out to God: Jeremiah 16:19 calls Him "my refuge in the day of distress," and Psalms 50:15 promises that God will deliver the one who calls upon Him.
H6869B.origine: The Hebrew word צָרָה comes from the root צר (tsar), which primarily means "to be narrow" or "to press." The basic image is that of oppression or constriction: one is literally in a tight spot, trapped, with no way out. Hence also comes the word צַר (tsar), which designates the enemy or adversary (the one who constricts you). Distress is therefore less an abstract emotion than a concrete state: one is trapped, under pressure, with no apparent escape.
H6869B.emploi: This word appears 69 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms, the Prophets, and the historical books. It describes various situations: the personal distress of Jacob or the psalmist in the face of peril or suffering (Genesis 35:3, Psalms 120:1), the collective distress of Israel oppressed by its enemies (Nehemiah 9:27), distress as a historical calamity (Jeremiah 30:7), or distress as a moral and spiritual crisis (Psalms 77:3). In all cases, distress is the context in which the faithful cry out to God: it drives one to prayer. The word is also used to describe the misfortunes sent by God in judgment (Isaiah 8:22) or to characterize the end times (Zephaniah 1:15).
H6869B.portee: Biblical distress is never a state without resources: it is always the moment when God intervenes for the one who calls upon Him. Meditating on this word helps the Christian understand that suffering and anguish, far from being signs of God's abandonment, are calls to cry out to Him. It is in distress that the faithful discover that God is their refuge and true support.

sens: woman who shares the bed of the same man and makes her a rival
one who annoys, troubles by jealousy or malice
H6869C.detail:
1. The word designates a woman who lives with another in the same house, sharing the same husband. She is a co-wife, a domestic rival in the context of ancient polygamous marriage. In 1 Samuel 1:6, Peninnah is the rival of Hannah: she lives under the same roof, married to the same man (Elkanah), and this daily proximity creates constant tension.

2. More broadly, a rival is one who annoys, torments out of jealousy or malice. She seeks to do harm, to vex, to irritate. Still in 1 Samuel 1:6, Peninnah "provokes" Hannah with mortifications, meaning she constantly troubles her out of jealous malice, hoping to make her bitter or hurt her.
H6869C.origine: The Hebrew word צָרָה (tsarah) comes from a root meaning "to press, squeeze, embrace" — the image of pressure, of oppression. A rival is literally one who "presses," who oppresses by her hostile presence. This same root produces words like צַר (tsar, "enemy, adversary") and צָרָה (tsarah, "distress, anguish"), as domestic rivalry creates emotional oppression.
H6869C.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Samuel 1:6. There it designates Peninnah, Elkanah's other wife, who cruelly and jealously harassed Hannah. The context is that of polygamous marriage, where the cohabitation of multiple wives created tensions, especially when one was barren and the other fertile. Peninnah took advantage of Hannah's infertility to torment her regularly, particularly during religious festivals. This unique account shows the rival as a figure of domestic malice, acting out of jealousy and wickedness.
H6869C.portee: This story reveals the hidden pain behind certain rivalries, including the most petty. Hannah suffered doubly: from her infertility and from the constant harassment of her rival. The Bible does not ignore the wounds that people inflict on each other out of envy, but it also shows that Hannah found her recourse in God alone, in silent prayer (1 Samuel 1:12-13). For the believer, it is a reminder that even the most humiliating relational torments can become the path to a deeper encounter with God.

sens: Woman of the united kingdom era, sister of King David
Mother of David's three great generals: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel
H6870.detail: Zeruiah is a woman from the time of King David, daughter of Jesse and sister of David himself (1 Samuel 26:6). She is best known as the mother of three of the greatest warriors of the kingdom: Joab, who commanded the army of Israel (2 Samuel 8:16), Abishai, who saved David's life against the Philistines (2 Samuel 21:17), and Asahel, the fastest runner among all the fighters (2 Samuel 2:18). Her name appears 26 times in the Old Testament, almost always to designate the sons of Zeruiah, showing the importance of this lineage in the military and political life of Israel under David.
H6870.origine: The name Zeruiah (צְרוּיָה) literally means "balm" or "God's balm": it evokes a fragrant plant, perhaps wormwood or an aromatic herb. It is a typical Hebrew name from the royal period, formed with the root צְרוּ (a plant) and the divine suffix יָה (God). This name reflects the importance attributed to this woman in the national life of Israel.
H6870.emploi: Zeruiah appears 26 times in the accounts of the Old Testament, mainly in the books of Samuel, Kings, and Chronicles. She is never the main subject of an action: she is always mentioned in relation to her sons, particularly Joab. The texts present her as the mother of the three most prominent military heroes of David's reign. She is thus linked to all the major military events of the kingdom — the capture of Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 11:6), the wars against Israel's enemies, and the internal conflicts of the royal court. She embodies a line of warriors whose legacy marks the entire reign of David and beyond.
H6870.portee: Zeruiah reminds us that in the eyes of the Bible, even minor figures play a role in God's design. Mother of three men, including Joab, the formidable commander of the army, she shows how God uses entire families to accomplish His plans. Her sons are powerful warriors, but also capable of cruelty (1 Kings 2:5): this invites us to see that human strength, even in the service of a pious king, must be submitted to God.

sens: Woman of Israel during the time of the united monarchy
Widow and mother of Jeroboam
H6871.detail: Tserua is a widow of Israel living during the time of Solomon. She is the mother of Jeroboam, who will later become king of the northern kingdom (Israel) after the division of the monarchy (1 Kings 11:26).
H6871.origine: The Hebrew name צְרוּעָה (Tserua) literally means "full-breasted" or "well-developed," but this literal meaning holds no particular significance in the biblical narrative. It is an ordinary Hebrew feminine name, borne by this mother whose only biblical mention is in the context of the birth and career of her illustrious son.
H6871.emploi: Tserua appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Kings 11:26. She is mentioned solely as the mother of Jeroboam, Solomon's servant who will rebel against the king and establish the northern kingdom after Solomon's death. Her status as a widow indicates that she lost her husband Nebat before Jeroboam became a significant figure. She remains a secondary figure, known primarily through the importance of her son in the history of Israel.
H6871.portee: The role of Tserua reminds us that the great actors in biblical history have mothers. Although her name appears only once, she is the mother of the one who caused the division of the kingdom of Israel, showing how a humble person can be connected to significant changes in divine history.

sens: Bag or pouch containing something wrapped
Set of things tied or gathered together
Bouquet of plants or flowers
H6872A.detail:
1. The primary meaning is a bag, a closed pouch where things are carried — like the money pouch of each of Jacob's sons, hidden in his grain sack (Genesis 42:35), or the money bag that the libertine takes to the adulterous woman (Proverbs 7:20). It is a closed, tight, attached container.
2. By extension, it refers to a set of things gathered and tied together: Job speaks of his transgressions "sealed in a package" (Job 14:17), as if they were tied together and kept; likewise, in 1 Samuel 25:29, the soul of the faithful is "bound in the bundle of the living with the Lord," an image of protection where the elect are gathered and held tightly in God's hand.
3. More broadly, it is a bouquet: the myrrh in the Song of Songs is a "bundle" that rests on the heart (Song of Songs 1:13), a group of flowers or aromatic herbs tied together.
H6872A.origine: The Hebrew word צְרוֹר (tseror) comes from a root meaning "to bind," "to tighten," "to enclose." The basic image is that of tightening, of what is knotted or firmly attached. A package is what is bound, condensed, gathered into a compact whole. This root is found in other Hebrew words of the same family that express the idea of limitation or confinement.
H6872A.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the Hebrew Bible. In Genesis 42:35, it is a bag containing money, a concrete and everyday object. In 1 Samuel 25:29 and Job 14:17, it takes on a figurative meaning: the bound soul, the sins gathered like in a closed package — the image becomes one of solid unity, protected or enclosed. In Proverbs 7:20 and Haggai 1:6, it is again a bag or pouch of money. In Song of Songs 1:13, it is a fragrant bouquet. The word thus oscillates between the material sense (a container, a package of goods) and the figurative sense (a gathered, protected, or imprisoned set).
H6872A.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the security that God offers: the soul bound "in the bundle of the living with the Lord" evokes absolute protection, an integrity preserved under the hand of the Lord. Conversely, the image of sealed sins in a package reminds us that nothing escapes God: our transgressions are counted and kept before Him. It is a call to trust and responsibility.

sens: Small pebble or grain of stone
Figuratively: fine grain, particle of matter
H6872B.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a small stone, a rock that can be held or moved. In 2 Samuel 17:13, it refers to tiny stones: the text imagines that if a city withdraws into a fortified position, "all Israel will bring ropes to that city" to destroy it until there remains "not a single stone" — meaning that even the smallest gravel will be removed, symbolizing total annihilation.
2. By extension, the word evokes any fine grain or particle. In Amos 9:9, God says: "I will shake the house of Israel among all nations, as one shakes with a sieve, so that not a single grain falls to the ground" — here, the word translated "grain" refers to the small stones that remain at the bottom of the sieve, an image of the remnant that God preserves despite judgment.
H6872B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to enclose" or "to tighten" (צרר): a stone is primarily a compact, hard material. The plural or derived forms retain this idea of smallness and density. The image is found in other Hebrew words of the same family, all related to what is narrow, pressed, or tightened.
H6872B.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In 2 Samuel 17:13, it refers to a stone in the literal sense: a small projectile that cannot be left to remain. In Amos 9:9, it is a grain in the figurative sense: the particles that remain in the sieve after sifting. In both cases, the emphasis is on smallness and multiplicity: elements so tiny that they symbolize either exhaustive destruction or the survival of the remnant.
H6872B.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on divine justice through two opposing but complementary images. In 2 Samuel, it reminds us that God's judgment is total and merciless toward the enemy. In Amos, it comforts the remnant of Israel: even if the people undergo the sifting of judgment, like grains in a sieve, none are lost from the fate that God reserves for His elect. These two aspects — judgment and preservation — show how God acts according to His justice and mercy.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the time of the united monarchy
H6872C.detail: 1. Tseror is an ancestor of King Saul, belonging to the tribe of Benjamin. He is the father of Becorath and the grandfather of Kish, who is the father of Saul (1 Samuel 9:1). He represents a lineage of important figures in the history of Israel, although he himself is mentioned only once in the Bible.
H6872C.origine: The name Tseror literally means "package" or "bundle" in Hebrew. It likely refers to a tied or wrapped object, but its use as a personal name remains enigmatic. It is a hereditary patronymic, like many names in biblical genealogies.
H6872C.emploi: Tseror appears only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Samuel 9:1, in a complete genealogy of King Saul. This passage establishes the royal lineage by tracing back through Kish, Abiel, Becorath to Tseror. His only role is genealogical: to show the family origins of Israel's first anointed king.

sens: To let out a loud and piercing cry
To make one's voice heard with strength and clarity
War cry, battle cry
To manifest one's power through voice
H6873.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to an animal or human cry: a loud, piercing, and clear sound, like the roar of a lion. It is a voice that carries far and imposes itself on the ear.

2. In a military context, it is the war cry uttered by a fighter: Zephaniah 1:14 speaks of the hero who "gives bitter cries," this cry that accompanies the attack and battle.

3. Biblically, it is also how God manifests His presence and strength: in Isaiah 42:13, the Lord "raises His voice, He gives cries" to show His fervor against His enemies. The cry becomes the very expression of power in action.
H6873.origine: The verb צָרַח comes from a root that evokes a high-pitched and piercing sound, the onomatopoeia of a natural cry. It is a simple and direct verb: it imitates the noise it describes. The word belongs to the Hebrew vocabulary of loud sounds and intense emotions.
H6873.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible. In Isaiah 42:13, it is God Himself who cries out to manifest His warrior strength against His enemies: His cry is the sign of His commitment to battle. In Zephaniah 1:14, it is the human hero who gives bitter cries on the day of the Lord, in a scene of terror and judgment. In both cases, the cry expresses power, combat, or the intense emotion of the moment.
H6873.portee: This word reminds us that God's voice is never silent or distant: it manifests itself with strength and clarity in history. When God "cries," it is to act, to combat evil, and to make Himself heard. For the believer, this encourages listening to the voice of the Lord that resounds with authority.

sens: Son of Jeduthun, Levitical musician in the time of David
H6874.detail: Tseri is a musician from the tribe of Levi, son of Jeduthun, who served at the court of King David. He was part of the sons of Jeduthun mentioned in 1 Chronicles 25:3 as musicians of the temple, responsible for praising and celebrating the Lord with instruments and song. His name also appears in the form "Izri" in 1 Chronicles 25:11.
H6874.origine: The name Tseri means "built" or "established" in Hebrew. It is a proper name designating a Levite from the family of Jeduthun, chief musician of the temple during the time of King David.
H6874.emploi: Tseri is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 25:3. He belonged to the musical family of Jeduthun, one of the three leaders of the temple musicians (along with Asaph and Heman). He was one of the six sons of Jeduthun listed to participate in sacrifices and praise, playing a prominent role in the public worship of the united kingdom of Israel.

sens: Resinous and fragrant substance extracted from trees, used to heal wounds and diseases
Commercial product exchanged between peoples
Remedy hoped to bring healing, image of help brought to suffering
H6875.detail:
1. Balm is a substance that flows from trees or is extracted: it is thick, fragrant, and oily. It is used to heal wounds and diseases, like an ointment or medicine (Jeremiah 46:11: "Take balm for her wound"). It was a rare and precious product.
2. Balm was a major trade item between the East and Egypt. The Ishmaelite merchants passing by Joseph were transporting balm, myrrh, and spices to sell in Egypt (Genesis 37:25). Israel also exported it: "They exchanged wheat... for your merchandise" of balm (Ezekiel 27:17).
3. Spiritually, Jeremiah uses balm as an image of the help that only God can provide: "Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician?" (Jeremiah 8:22). Balm represents everything that could heal, but without God, even the best remedies are insufficient.
H6875.origine: The word designates a substance that heals and soothes, which explains its figurative use for consolation. In Hebrew, balm comes from Gilead, a region known for its aromatic trees and water sources. This balm was rare, precious, and highly sought after: that is why it became an item of international trade and a biblical image of relief and hope.
H6875.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the Old Testament. First as a concrete merchandise (Genesis 37:25, Genesis 43:11, Ezekiel 27:17), where it is among the riches of the Near East along with myrrh, honey, and spices. Then in the prophecies of Jeremiah, balm becomes an image: of the futility of human remedies without God (Jeremiah 8:22, Jeremiah 46:11) and of the incurable wound inflicted by sin (Jeremiah 51:8, where Babylon needs it but will not be healed). Balm thus transitions from the concrete to the spiritual.
H6875.portee: This progression of the word—from precious merchandise to the image of divine help—teaches the reader that earthly resources, even the best, are not enough to heal the rupture caused by sin. Only God can offer us the true "balm": reconciliation and peace. It is an invitation to seek in Him, not in false remedies, true healing.

sens: Inhabitant or native of Tyre
Merchant or artisan from Tyre
What is characteristic of Tyre, its products or know-how
H6876.detail:
1. A Tyrian is a person from Tyre, the great Phoenician port city. Several important Tyrians appear in biblical history: the father of the master craftsman Hiram who worked for King Solomon was Tyrian (1 Kings 7:14), and Huram-Abi, son of a Tyrian father, was the genius craftsman who oversaw all the bronze, gold, and silver work of Solomon's temple (2 Chronicles 2:14).
2. The Tyrians are often mentioned as merchants and suppliers of precious wood. They brought cedar wood from Lebanon to David (1 Chronicles 22:4), and they also provided it during the reconstruction of the temple after the exile (Ezra 3:7). In the time of Nehemiah, Tyrians had settled in Jerusalem to sell fish and various goods (Nehemiah 13:16).
3. The Tyrians embody artisanal and commercial know-how: skilled in working with precious metals, sculpture, dyeing, and maritime trade. Their reputation for skill was such that they were called upon for major royal and religious projects in Israel.
H6876.origine: The word comes from Tyre (צֹר in Hebrew), the name of the famous Phoenician city. Tyre literally means "the Rock" or "the Cliff," as it was built on a rocky island in the Mediterranean. The adjective Tyrian (צֹרִי) simply designates "one who belongs to Tyre" or "one who is from Tyre." The Hebrew suffix -ִי (-i) creates this adjective of origin.
H6876.emploi: The word צֹרִי appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the books of Kings and Chronicles or after the exile. The Tyrians are presented as important commercial and artisanal partners for Israel and Judah: they provide cedar from Lebanon, construction wood, and their master craftsmen participate in major works. Hiram and Huram-Abi, both sons of Tyrian fathers, are prominent figures of technical expertise. Later, in the post-exilic period, the Tyrians are established merchants in Jerusalem, which raises some religious concerns regarding Sabbath exchanges (Nehemiah 13:16). The neutral or positive term in the early contexts becomes slightly critical when it comes to the profane commerce of the Sabbath.
H6876.portee: The Tyrians in the Bible remind us that God has endowed foreign nations with extraordinary skills and riches—the Phoenicians of Tyre for metalwork, rare wood, and art—that He can put to the service of His people and His temple. This also shows that Israel's faith was built in relation to the surrounding world, without complete isolation. However, the later mention of the Tyrians as Sabbath merchants also highlights the temptations of compromise with idolatrous and worldly commerce.

sens: Fortified structure serving as a refuge or last stronghold
Chamber or underground excavation dug into the earth or rock
Tower or defensive post where one can take refuge in times of danger
H6877.detail: 1. The word primarily designates a fortified structure where one can protect themselves during an attack. In Shechem, all the inhabitants take refuge in the "fortress" of the house of the god Berith (Judges 9:46), a closed and defensible place where they believe they will find safety — until Abimelech sets it on fire (Judges 9:49). 2. The term also evokes an excavation or underground chamber, dug into the rock or earth for hiding and protection. In 1 Samuel 13:6, the men of Israel, closely pressed by the enemy, hide in caves and "towers," seeking refuge in underground or fortified places. 3. By extension, the word can simply refer to a high post or tower from which one can defend or observe.
H6877.origine: The Hebrew root is close to the idea of a cry or piercing sound (צרח tsa-rah, "to cry"), which could evoke a place from which one cries out for alarm. The word is also related to terms designating fortified refuges. The exact meaning remains partially uncertain, but biblical usage clearly shows that it is a place of defense and protection.
H6877.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always to describe a defensive refuge. Two occurrences are found in the episode of Shechem (Judges 9:46-49), where the "fortress" is the last bastion of the inhabitants against Abimelech. One occurrence in 1 Samuel 13:6 designates the remote and protected places where the Israelites hide in the face of the Philistine invasion. In all cases, the word evokes a situation of extreme danger where one must quickly take refuge. The translation varies between "fortress," "tower," and "cave" depending on the immediate context.
H6877.portee: This word speaks to the heart of the Christian about the meaning of true refuge. In rereading these accounts, we see that human fortresses — even the sanctuary of Shechem — do not save those who refuse to turn to God. The Bible invites the believer to seek in God alone a refuge more secure than any wall of stone or earth.

sens: What is lacking and necessary for living or accomplishing a task
Concrete requirement that must be met
H6878.detail:
1. Need is what is indispensable for existence or action: in the only biblical example, King Solomon expresses to Hiram of Tyre how much wood from Lebanon he needs to build the Temple (2 Chronicles 2:16 — "as much as you will need"). It is a material and concrete necessity, a required quantity to successfully carry out a work.
2. In a broader sense, this word designates any requirement or request that must be satisfied — the need of the moment, what is imposed upon us by circumstances or reason.
H6878.origine: The Hebrew word צֹרֶךְ comes from a root that expresses the idea of "pressing," "tightening," "demanding." It is related to the verb צָרַךְ which means "to need" or "to urgently request." The starting image is one of constraint, an urgency that presses on a person and forces them to act. In biblical Aramaic, a similar form is found. It is a rare word in biblical Hebrew, but it clearly expresses the essence of need: not a desire or want, but a necessity that imposes itself.
H6878.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Chronicles 2:16. It is a crucial moment: Solomon negotiates with Hiram, king of Tyre, to obtain the necessary cedar wood for the construction of the Temple. The phrase "as much as you will need" expresses the indispensable material quantity for the project. It is practical, administrative vocabulary that emphasizes the concrete and inevitable aspect of necessity. The word does not carry any particular spiritual or moral connotation, but remains anchored in economic and constructive reality.
H6878.portee: This word reminds us that God recognizes the legitimate material needs of His people. When Solomon expresses his needs to Hiram to build the Temple, it is to accomplish the work that God has entrusted to him. This invites us to distinguish true need from mere covetousness, and to honestly ask for what is necessary to serve God and build His kingdom.

sens: Contagious disease characterized by skin sores and lesions
State of one who suffers from this disease
Condition of ritual impurity and social exclusion that results from it
H6879.detail:
1. Leprosy is a serious disease that manifests as white patches and lesions on the skin. In Exodus 4:6, Moses' hand becomes "covered with leprosy, white as snow" — the image describes the distinctive and recognizable appearance of the disease.
2. One who is afflicted becomes "leprous," separated from the community. Naaman is described as "mighty and valiant" but "leprous" (2 Kings 5:1): his condition affects his social status despite his military authority.
3. Leprosy renders one ritually impure: it leads to exclusion from the camp and mandatory isolation. In Leviticus 14:2, the leprous person must be examined and purified by the priest before rejoining the community. The four lepers in 2 Kings 7:3 are "at the entrance of the gate," relegated outside, waiting for death.
H6879.origine: The verb צָרַע (tsara) comes from a root that expresses the idea of being afflicted or separated. It is linked to the condition of impurity in the Mosaic law. In Hebrew, the forms of the verb describe both the disease itself (the passive state of the afflicted) and the visible lesions that characterize it. Biblical leprosy likely encompasses several serious skin conditions, all treated according to the Levitical code of impurity.
H6879.emploi: This word appears 18 times in the Old Testament, concentrated in the law of purification (Leviticus 13—14) and in historical accounts relating famous cases. Naaman the Syrian (2 Kings 5) and King Uzziah of Judah (2 Chronicles 26:20-21) are the most developed examples: both are figures of power struck by this disease, highlighting the impartial nature of divine judgment. The word designates both the physical disease and the religious status of impurity that results from it, and its use varies depending on whether one describes the appearance of the disease, the state of the sick person, or the purification rites.
H6879.portee: Leprosy in the Bible symbolizes impurity and separation, both physical and spiritual. It reminds us that serious illness, far from respecting human status or power, can humiliate the greatest. It also illustrates divine mercy: Naaman is healed by the word of the prophet Elisha, showing that even the most extreme impurity does not escape God's grace. For the believer, it is an invitation to recognize one's need for purification and restoration by God.

sens: large, venomous flying insect of the wasp family
instrument of God's anger to drive out the enemies of Israel
H6880.detail:
1. The hornet is a flying insect resembling a large wasp, capable of stinging and causing harm. It is a feared and harmful creature. The Bible only mentions it in a figurative sense, never to describe it in itself.

2. God uses hornets as a living weapon to drive out the enemy peoples occupying the promised land. This is not a poetic image: God literally sends hornets ("I will send hornets ahead of you," Exodus 23:28; "I sent hornets ahead of you," Joshua 24:12). It is a supernatural act of deliverance. The hornet here symbolizes the unpredictable and inevitable power of God that terrifies and drives out His enemies without the people needing to fight themselves.
H6880.origine: The Hebrew word צִרְעָה (tsiréah) specifically refers to the hornet, this winged insect. Its etymology is uncertain, but the word appears exclusively in the three passages where God sends hornets before the conquest. There are no other Hebrew words for the insect: the Bible always uses this precise term, which emphasizes the flying and venomous nature of the creature.
H6880.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Bible, always to evoke a supernatural act of God. In Exodus 23:28, God promises to send hornets to drive out the Hivites, Canaanites, and Hittites. In Deuteronomy 7:20, He renews this promise by saying He will send hornets "until the destruction of those who escape." In Joshua 24:12, Joshua reminds the people that God kept His word: "I sent hornets ahead of you, which drove them out from before you." These three uses show the hornet as the direct agent of Israel's victory, without human military intervention.
H6880.portee: This word reminds us that Israel's victory over its enemies does not come from its own strength, but from the power of God. The hornets symbolize the invisible and supernatural action of God that prepares the way for His people. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation to recognize that God fights for those who trust Him, and that His power is far superior to human strength and weapons.

sens: Fortified city of the tribe of Dan in ancient Palestine
H6881.detail: Zorah is a city located in the territory of Dan, in the southwest of the Promised Land. Its name literally means "wasp" or "hornet" in Hebrew, perhaps due to the abundant harmful insects in the region. It is most famous as the birthplace and residence of Samson: it is where his father Manoah is born (Judges 13:2), and after his death, Samson is buried there between Zorah and the nearby city of Eshtaol (Judges 16:31). The city also appears in the migration of the Danites in search of new territory: five valiant men depart from Zorah to explore the northern part of the land (Judges 18:2).
H6881.origine: The Hebrew word צׇרְעָה (tsor'ah) derives from a root meaning "wasp" or "hornet," feared insects that build their nests in warm, rocky areas. This descriptive name likely reflects the local geography or a notable characteristic of the territory. The city is also mentioned in 2 Chronicles and Nehemiah in different contexts, attesting to its lasting importance in the history of Israel.
H6881.emploi: Zorah is mentioned ten times in the Bible, primarily in the books of Joshua and Judges. It first appears in the allocation of territories among the tribes (Joshua 15:33 and 19:41), where it is assigned to Dan. It becomes especially famous through the story of Samson: it is where this judge of Israel, son of Manoah, is born, and it is between Zorah and Eshtaol that he is ultimately buried after his exploits. The city also serves as a starting point for the Danite explorers seeking better land (Judges 18:2, 8, 11). It is mentioned one last time as a fortified city of Judah under King Rehoboam (2 Chronicles 11:10) and in the list of inhabited localities after the exile (Nehemiah 11:29).
H6881.portee: Zorah reminds us that God's plans are fulfilled in specific, concrete, identifiable places. The life of Samson, the most extraordinary judge of Israel, is rooted in an ordinary little town: God often chooses humble origins. Samson's return to Zorah to be buried, after a life of power and falls, symbolizes the faithfulness of his family and the final rest that God grants to His servants.

sens: inhabitant of Zorah
H6882.detail: 1. The Zoreathites are the inhabitants of the city of Zorah, mentioned in the genealogies of the tribes of Israel. The text presents them as a family descended from Salma and from Kirjath-Jearim (1 Chronicles 2:53 and 2:54).
H6882.origine: The word comes from Zorah, a city whose name means "wasp" or "hornet" in Hebrew. The Zoreathites are therefore literally "the people of Zorah." The suffix -ite denotes belonging to a place, as with other peoples or families listed in these genealogies.
H6882.emploi: This term appears three times in the Bible, all in the book of Chronicles, in the genealogies of the tribes of Israel (1 Chronicles 2:53, 2:54, and 4:2). It designates a family or clan of Israel whose members were from or associated with the city of Zorah. The Bible provides no further details about their history or particular role; they are simply listed among the other Israelite families.

sens: serious and contagious skin disease characterized by spots and sores
trace of mold or mildew on clothing
trace of mold or mildew on the walls of a house
H6883.detail:
1. Leprosy is a serious skin disease that manifests as tumors, scabs, or white patches that progressively spread over the body (Leviticus 13:2, 13:12). It is a contagious disease that renders the person unclean according to the Law: they must be examined by the priest, isolated, and declared unclean if the sore spreads (Leviticus 13:27). Once healed, the person undergoes a purification rite with the sprinkling of the blood of a sacrifice and purifying water before being reintegrated into the community (Leviticus 14:7).
2. The word also refers to a spot of mold or mildew on clothing, presenting a greenish or reddish color (Leviticus 13:49). This defect renders the garment liable and must be shown to the priest for inspection (Leviticus 13:49).
3. It also applies to a trace of mold in the walls of a house, which contaminates the entire building until it is treated or the house is demolished (Leviticus 14:34).
H6883.origine: The Hebrew word tsâra'ath comes from a root that evokes the idea of contamination and separation. In the Law of Moses, leprosy symbolizes spiritual impurity and the rupture of communion with God and with the community of Israel. The concept extends beyond biological disease to become a sign of ritual separation.
H6883.emploi: The word appears 33 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in the purity laws of Leviticus (chapters 13 and 14) and Deuteronomy, which describe in detail how to identify, examine, and treat leprosy in people, clothing, and houses. It is also found in 2 Kings 5, where Naaman, a Syrian general, is afflicted with leprosy and seeks healing from the prophet Elisha (2 Kings 5:6, 5:27), and in 2 Chronicles 26:19, where King Uzziah contracts leprosy for having transgressed the boundaries of the priesthood. The disease is always treated as a sign of major impurity that imposes social and religious separation.
H6883.portee: Leprosy in Scripture teaches the believer that sin is like a contagious impurity that separates us from God and His community. It shows that only God can purify the sinner and reintegrate them into communion. For the Christian, leprosy becomes a powerful image of the need for forgiveness and spiritual transformation in Christ, who alone can make us pure and acceptable before God.

sens: To melt a metal to purify it from its dross and obtain the pure.
To treat a metal with fire to refine it and make it usable.
To subject someone or something to a test, a trial, to verify its quality or value.
To test the faith, heart, or intentions of someone to purify or reveal them.
H6884.detail:
1. The verb primarily refers to the work of molten metal in fire: silver or gold is heated to separate the dross and obtain pure and usable metal. Proverbs 25:4 expresses this well: "Remove the dross from the silver, and a vessel for the silversmith will emerge" — the process focuses on the metal itself, which passes through fire to be purified.
2. By extension, the verb also refers to the one who performs this work: the silversmith or refiner, the artisan who refines precious metals (Nehemiah 3:32: "The silversmiths worked"). The crucible is the utensil in which the metal is subjected to fire.
3. The meaning broadens to any testing: to test something or someone means to subject them to a trial to verify their strength, faithfulness, or value. Judges 7:4 speaks of making a "selection" of the people, that is, testing them to separate the strong from the weak.
4. When applied to God and individuals, the verb takes on a spiritual dimension: God "tests" the hearts and minds of men (Psalms 26:2) as one refines gold in fire, to reveal what they truly are and to purify them. It is a trial that cleanses or purifies.
H6884.origine: The Hebrew verb צָרַף (tsar-raph) comes from a root that evokes the work of fire and metal: to melt, to heat, to refine. The central image is that of fire which transforms and purifies. This same work of metal naturally applies to the figurative sense: everything that passes through fire to be made pure — faith, heart, promise — is "tested." The root belongs to the ancient vocabulary of precious metal work in Israel.
H6884.emploi: The verb appears 29 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms, Proverbs, and the Prophets. It is first used in a concrete sense: Isaiah 41:7 describes the refiner who works gold to make an idol. But very quickly, it takes on a spiritual meaning: God tests the faith of believers as one refines gold in fire. Psalms 66:10 says: "You have tested us as one tests gold in fire" — the trial is a purification. Jeremiah 9:7: "Behold, I will refine them and test them": God subjects His people to testing to purify or reveal them. The Word itself is "tested" (Psalms 119:140): it is as pure as gold refined seven times.
H6884.portee: This word enriches the biblical understanding of the trials that believers go through. The Bible does not see them as mere misfortunes, but as a fire that purifies and strengthens faith — a work of the Spirit in the heart, analogous to that of metal in fire. This gives meaning to suffering: it is God who refines and tests to reveal and purify what is true and solid in His child. It is an invitation to see trials not as a curse, but as grace.

sens: An artisan who works with gold and precious metals
One who makes or repairs objects of gold and silver
In a figurative sense: one who shapes with care and skill
H6885.detail:
1. The silversmith is a specialized artisan in the transformation of gold: he melts, shapes, and chisels it to create precious objects — cups, crowns, jewelry, objects of worship. In Nehemiah 3:31, the silversmiths are among those who rebuild the walls of Jerusalem, showing that Israel had artisans of this prestigious trade upon their return from exile.
2. By extension, the silversmith also works with silver and other precious metals. His skill in purifying, melting, and shaping metals makes him valuable in a society where precious objects hold great religious and economic significance.
3. The image of the silversmith symbolizes the delicacy and perfection of the work: in biblical literature, it often illustrates how God carefully shapes His people, or how He purifies like gold in fire.
H6885.origine: The Hebrew word צֹרְפִי (tsorphi) comes from the root צרף (tsaraf), which means "to refine, to purify (a metal)." This root evokes the action of subjecting metal to fire to purify it from its impurities. The word literally designates one who refines precious metals — the purifier, the refiner. It is a profession well known in the Bible, both for its religious applications (the objects of the tabernacle and the temple) and secular.
H6885.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Nehemiah 3:31. It is listed among the artisans who participated in the rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah's leadership, after the return from exile in Babylon. This context shows that silversmiths formed a recognized and organized professional class in Israel. Their presence among the builders reminds us that the rebuilt Jerusalem was to regain the splendor of its worship and institutions, which required the talents of these artisans.
H6885.portee: The mention of silversmiths among the builders of Jerusalem illustrates that the restoration of Israel after exile also involved the restoration of religious splendor and organized civic life. It reminds us that all trades and talents find their place in the work of reconstruction and in the service of God.

sens: Coastal city of Phoenicia, south of Sidon
Place of refuge for Elijah during the drought
Northern boundary of the restored territory of Israel in the prophetic vision
H6886.detail: 1. Zarephath is an ancient coastal city located in Phoenicia, on the Mediterranean coast south of the great city of Sidon. Its Hebrew name means "refinery" or "place of melting," possibly evoking the metallurgical activity of this port (1 Kings 17:9). 2. It is here that the prophet Elijah took refuge during the great drought sent by God upon Israel. God commanded him to go there to hide and be fed by a poor widow from the city (1 Kings 17:10) — a moment when he resurrected the son of this woman. 3. In the vision of restoration given to the prophet Obadiah, Zarephath marks the northern boundary of the territory that the children of Israel will reclaim (Obadiah 1:20), symbolizing the recovery of lands up to the ancient borders.
H6886.origine: The Hebrew name צָֽרְפַת (tsaraphath) literally means "refinery" or "foundry," derived from the root צָרַף (tsaraph), which means "to refine," "to purify metals." The Greek name of the city, Σάρεπτα (Sarepta), is the direct transcription of this Hebrew word. This name reflects the commercial and artisanal activity of this Phoenician port city.
H6886.emploi: Zarephath appears three times in the Hebrew Bible as a specific geographical site. It is most famous as the place of Elijah's miraculous refuge: God sends him there to escape the wrath of King Ahab, and it is there that a widow feeds him with flour and oil that do not run out (1 Kings 17:9-10). The prophet also performs the miracle of resurrecting the widow's son there. It reappears in the prophecy of Obadiah as a territorial boundary of Israel's return, indicating the extent of the future restoration of God's people.
H6886.portee: The story of Elijah at Zarephath demonstrates God's faithfulness in providing for His servants beyond the borders of Israel and performing miraculous signs to save and restore. It is a narrative that teaches trust in God during trials and the power of His Word to even spiritually resurrect the dead. For the Christian, it is a model of refuge in God and trust in His provision.

sens: To wrap or attach something by compressing it
To put in tightness, confinement
To experience a sensation of tightness or lack
To besiege a city or fortified place
To press someone oppressively, to overwhelm
To be closely tied to someone or something
H6887B.detail:
1. To wrap or attach something by compressing it: this is the simplest physical idea — taking something and compressing it to wrap or secure it tightly. The Israelites during the Exodus "wrap" their unleavened dough in clothing by binding it (Exodus 12:34), just as one would tie a burden for transport.

2. To put in tightness or confinement: a place where one is confined, closed off. David confines his ten concubines in a "secluded" place, evoking an imposed tightness, a soft prison (2 Samuel 20:3).

3. To experience a sensation of tightness, confinement, or lack: when a person is "in distress," they feel compressed, suffocated by circumstances, with no way out (Psalms 31:10; 2 Chronicles 28:22). It is the heart that tightens.

4. To besiege a city: the enemy army surrounds and compresses the place, pressing it from all sides, cutting off its resources and exits. This is the military application of the idea of confinement.

5. To press someone oppressively, to overwhelm: to weigh upon them with a burden or threat that suffocates. Enemies who "pursue" someone morally bind them.

6. To be closely tied to someone: in poetic language, the "soul bound in the bundle of the living" (1 Samuel 25:29) evokes an indissoluble solidarity, like things tied together.
H6887B.origine: The verb צָרַר (tsa.rar) comes from a root meaning "narrow," "tight." The word הִ֗צַּר (ha-tsar, "the narrow"), a noun derived from it, also appears in the Bible. The fundamental image is that of compression, tightness: something that takes up little space, that confines or oppresses. In Hebrew, the root אתֶר (tsar) has also given rise to צָר (tsar, "the adversary," literally "the one who compresses"), and צָרָה (tsa-rah, "distress"). It is a simple and concrete verb: what is narrow, what compresses, what suffocates.
H6887B.emploi: This verb appears 22 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical narratives, psalms, and proverbs. Its uses distribute according to several nuances: physical binding (Exodus 12:34 — to wrap), confinement (2 Samuel 20:3 — to sequester), moral or spiritual distress (Psalms 31:10; 2 Chronicles 28:22), military siege (Deuteronomy 28:52 implied by context), and close friendship or alliance (1 Samuel 25:29 — the bound soul). The word is also used in the passive to express suffering endured. In poetic texts, it takes on a more figurative hue: "to bind the waters in his garment" (Proverbs 30:4) is an image of divine mastery. It is a word of both concrete (physical action) and emotional (inner sensation) registers.
H6887B.portee: This word reminds the reader that distress, whether physical, social, or spiritual, is an experience of tightness and compression. It also teaches that God can "bind" the souls of His faithful — not in oppression, but in safety and alliance. The notion of siege reveals how the enemy (visible or invisible) can confine and suffocate; it invites seeking refuge in God. Finally, the figurative use of the verb enriches biblical prayer: expressing suffering as a physical sensation of tightness makes supplication more touching and true.

sens: State of intense anguish or pain in the face of danger or suffering
Physical or moral torment
Anguish of a woman giving birth, acute and unavoidable suffering
H6887C.detail:
1. The word describes a situation of danger or misfortune that provokes a reaction of anguish. It is the state of the psalmist who cries out to God in difficult moments: "Do not hide your face from me in the day of my distress" (Psalms 102:3). The image is that of a person being squeezed, pressed by circumstances, seeking refuge.
2. The word also evokes the inner torment that accompanies suffering, especially when one feels abandoned or threatened. The emphasis is on the psychic and physical reality of the evil one endures, not on a mere passing discomfort.
3. Distress can also refer to the acute pains that accompany childbirth or a great crisis: "the heart of the heroes of Moab is in this day like the heart of a woman in labor" (Jeremiah 48:41). This image of the woman in labor expresses a suffering that rises, that tightens, inevitable and relentless.
H6887C.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to squeeze," "to press." This root evokes the idea of constriction, of pressure that confines. That is why distress is often represented as a state where one feels tightly pressed by circumstances — by danger, illness, fear, or persecution. The word translates an experience that is both physical and emotional: that of feeling squeezed on all sides.
H6887C.emploi: This Hebrew verb appears four times in the Bible. Two occurrences are found in the Psalms, where the psalmist calls for help in times of personal distress (59:17 and 102:3), suggesting a context of danger or persecution. The other two occurrences, in Jeremiah, metaphorically describe the hearts of the Moabite and Edomite warriors at the moment they learn of their military defeat, comparing them to a woman in labor (48:41 and 49:22). The word captures each time an acute, intense suffering that is difficult to bear.
H6887C.portee: This word helps the believer to recognize and name their own suffering honestly before God. The Psalms show that it is acceptable to cry out to God in the midst of distress, without hiding one's anguish or pretending that everything is fine. It is a word that gives voice to the reality of evil and fear, while opening the way to calling upon God for refuge and help.

sens: one who shows hostility, who fights against someone
one who oppresses, who persecutes
one who vexes, who torments
the opponent in a conflict
one who harms, who does evil
H6887D.detail:
1. The most direct meaning is that of a person or people who show active hostility: a fighter, a military or political adversary. In Exodus 23:22, God promises to be "the enemy of your enemies," which clearly refers to the hostile peoples against Israel.
2. By extension, the word refers to one who oppresses or persecutes: someone who intentionally does harm, who crushes. In Psalm 129:1, Israel says, "They have greatly oppressed me from my youth," evoking a constant pressure.
3. More broadly, it refers to one who torments or vexes, causing moral or physical suffering. In Psalm 42:11, the psalmist speaks of his "persecutors" who hurt him with their words.
4. The word can also simply refer to the opponent in a conflict, one who opposes or resists. This is the idea in Psalm 8:3, where it speaks of "confounding your adversaries."
5. Finally, it refers to one who harms, who causes damage or loss. Esther 9:24 shows Haman as the "enemy of all the Jews" because he seeks their destruction.
H6887D.origine: The Hebrew root צרר (tsa.rar) expresses the idea of tightening, embracing, oppressing. It appears in several forms: צַר (tsar, "narrow"), צָרָה (tsa.rah, "distress"), and עַצְרוּת (a.tse.rout, "obstruction"). The enemy is literally one who "tightens" or "oppresses" — who suffocates his opponent. The family of this word is rich in terms of hostility and suffering: it depicts hostility as pressure, constriction.
H6887D.emploi: This verb appears 25 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the Psalms (where it often describes the oppression suffered by the faithful) and also in the historical books, notably in Esther where it qualifies Haman. The word is particularly frequent in the prayers and laments of the psalmist: it expresses the concrete experience of being pressed, attacked, pursued. In Numbers 33:55, the Canaanites that the Israelites do not drive out will become their "enemies," a perpetual threat. In the Psalms, the enemy is often invisible or distant, but always threatening: it is the figure of one who watches, who oppresses, who must be delivered to God's justice. The word thus encompasses both open hostility and insidious persecution.
H6887D.portee: This word reminds the believer that hostility exists in this world — it is real, it hurts, it oppresses. But the Bible names it and places it before God: the psalms teach to present one's enemies to God, not to take revenge oneself, and to trust in His justice. By praying about the enemy, the believer does not remain a prisoner of it; he entrusts the judgment to God. It is an invitation to spiritual clarity: to recognize hostility for what it is and to place it in the hands of the Lord.

sens: To provoke jealousy and competition between two wives or two women
To create tension by putting two people in competition
To incite hostility through unequal favors or preferences
H6887E.detail:
1. The verb speaks of a situation where a man has multiple wives and creates jealousy between them by putting them in competition. In Mosaic Law, it is forbidden to take the sister of one's wife to avoid creating this painful rivalry: "You shall not take your wife's sister, to provoke rivalry" (Leviticus 18:18). The word evokes bitterness, pain, and conflict that arise when a woman fears losing her husband's affection or possessions to another.
2. More broadly, the verb expresses the idea of putting someone in a lower position or offending them in favor of a rival. It is an action that intentionally or unintentionally hurts, creating unjust inequalities.
H6887E.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that carries the idea of tightening, embracing, from which the image of tension and distress arises. In Hebrew, the same root gives "tsarar" (צרר), which also means "to afflict" or "to torment." The underlying idea is that of pressure, the embrace that causes suffering — rivalry being precisely an emotional pressure that oppresses.
H6887E.emploi: The verb appears only once in the biblical text, in Leviticus 18:18, in the context of the marriage prohibitions stated by Moses. The Law establishes that taking two sisters creates a destructive rivalry, and thus the prohibition. This unique usage shows that the Bible takes emotional wounds and family conflicts seriously, and that it regulates unions to protect domestic peace.
H6887E.portee: This word reminds the believer that God cares about peace and harmony in the family. It shows that jealousy and rivalry are not neutral feelings: they cause serious harm. For the Christian, this invites avoiding situations that provoke envy or competition among loved ones, and to seek fairness and kindness in human relationships.

sens: Location in the West Bank, in the territory of Manasseh
H6888.detail: 1. Tsererah is a city or region in the territory of Manasseh, in the Promised Land. It appears in Judges 7:22 as the point of flight for the Midianites pursued by Gideon and his three hundred men after their miraculous defeat in battle: "The camp fled to Beth-Shittah toward Tsererah, to the border of Abel-Meholah near Tabbath." It was a site located on the route of retreat, between the Jezreel Valley and the Jordan.
H6888.origine: The name Tsererah comes from Hebrew and literally means "oppression." It is related to Tseredah (or Zeredah in French) and Zarethan (Zarethan), other forms or variants of the same place. These different spellings likely refer to the same locality or very close localities in the same region.
H6888.emploi: Tsererah appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 7:22. It is mentioned as a geographical landmark during the pursuit of the Midianites by Gideon's army, marking the trajectory of their flight toward the Jordan. This mention informs us about the geography of the Promised Land and the extent of the territory traversed during Israel's wars against its enemies.

sens: Man from the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H6889.detail: Tséreth is a man from the tribe of Judah living during the divided monarchy (between the 10th and 6th centuries B.C.). He is the son of Ashur, the founder of Tekoa, and his wife Helea. He appears in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles 4:7, where he is mentioned alongside his brothers Zohar and Ethnan. His name means "splendor" in Hebrew.
H6889.origine: The name Tséreth comes from Hebrew and means "splendor." It belongs to the lineage of Ashur, founder of the city of Tekoa, located in Judea. Like many Hebrew names, it evokes a quality or characteristic that is valued: splendor, brilliance, or radiance. This name fits within the genealogical tradition of Judah, where each name recalls a virtue or remarkable trait.
H6889.emploi: Tséreth appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:7. He is listed in a genealogical record of the clan of Judah, enumerated among the descendants of Ashur and Helea. This unique mention suggests that Tséreth did not play a major role in biblical history, but that he deserved to be recorded in the genealogical memory of the people of Judah. The Chronicles place great importance on these lists of names, which establish the continuity and legitimacy of each clan.

sens: City of the tribe of Reuben, in Transjordan
H6890.detail: Tséreth-Haschachar is a city located in the territory assigned to the tribe of Reuben, east of the Jordan River. Its name means "splendor of the dawn" in Hebrew, likely evoking the beauty of its heights at sunrise. It is mentioned in Joshua 13:19 among the cities and villages of Reuben, listed during the division of the lands among the tribes of Israel after the conquest of Canaan.
H6890.origine: The Hebrew name צֶרֶת הַשַּׁחַר (tséreth hash-shachar) is composed of two elements: צֶרֶת (tséreth), which means "splendor" or "brightness," and הַשַּׁחַר (hash-shachar), "the dawn" or "the rising of the day." This name describes the place by its luminous appearance in the morning, a common characteristic of place names in Israel that reflect geography or remarkable natural phenomena.
H6890.emploi: Tséreth-Haschachar appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 13:19, where it is listed among the cities of the tribe of Reuben. It is included in the list of territorial inheritances given to each tribe after the conquest of Canaan, alongside Kirjathaim and Sibmah. Its unique mention in the context of land division shows its administrative and geographical importance in the organization of the Reubenite territory.

sens: City in the Jordan Valley where the river stopped during Israel's crossing
Region or locality near the Jordan, serving as a geographical landmark
H6891.detail:
1. Tsarthan is a city located in the Jordan Valley, famous for the miracle of the parting of the waters: when Israel crossed the Jordan to conquer Canaan, the waters of the river stopped and rose in a heap near the city of Adam, next to Tsarthan (Joshua 3:16). It is at this precise location that the great miracle occurred, while the people passed over on dry ground opposite Jericho.
2. Tsarthan also appears as a geographical landmark in the administrative and economic region of ancient Jordan: it is mentioned near Beth-Shean as the boundary of the territory of one of King Solomon's officials (1 Kings 4:12), and it is cited as a region of fertile plain where the king made bronze objects for the temple, between Succoth and Tsarthan (1 Kings 7:46).
H6891.origine: The Hebrew name צָרְתָן (Tsarthan) literally means "their distress" or "their trouble," probably referring to the difficult circumstances associated with this place or its history. The meaning of the name seems to memorialize the context of the crossing of the Jordan — a critical moment when Israel had to confront the formidable river. Although the etymology is ancient and the place historical, the name has retained its original form throughout biblical history.
H6891.emploi: Tsarthan appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. First and foremost in the foundational account of Joshua 3:16, where it marks the precise location of the miracle of the Jordan stopping to allow Israel to pass — a central event in the conquest of Canaan. Then, it appears in the territorial administration of the united kingdom, in 1 Kings 4:12, as a geographical landmark of the Jordan region. Finally, in 1 Kings 7:46, it is mentioned as a site for making bronze objects for the temple, in the fertile plain of the Jordan. Tsarthan is thus both a site of Israel's foundational miracle and an economic center of the Jordan plain during Solomon's time.

sens: What an animal or person expels from their stomach through the mouth
Figuratively, what one abandons and then returns to, what one recidivates
H6892A.detail:
1. Vomit is literally the matter that the stomach expels — here, it is what a dog has rejected. The image is crude but familiar to a biblical reader: it serves to illustrate something repugnant, unclean.
2. Figuratively, vomit symbolizes what one has once left or what one abhors: in Proverbs 26:11, the dog that returns to its vomit represents the fool who returns to his folly — he abandons wisdom as one rejects what is filthy, only to plunge back into it, which is profoundly unnatural.
H6892A.origine: The word קֵא (qe) is a variant of the verb קִיא (qia, "to vomit"). In Hebrew, the root simply evokes the act of regurgitating. The nominal form designates the product of this act. It is a concrete word, without etymological mystery: it paints the raw image of what the body expels.
H6892A.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 26:11. Solomon uses it in a memorable comparison: as a dog returning to its vomit is absurd, so is a fool returning to his folly. The image, although repugnant, powerfully struck the mind of the ancient reader, accustomed to observing animal behavior. It illustrates how one can know folly and return to it — as if one were voluntarily returning to what one has rejected with disgust.
H6892A.portee: This image of vomit will resonate with every Christian aware of sin: it illustrates the absurdity of falling back into the evil one has abandoned. It invites maintaining a lasting distance from what one has recognized as bad, and not to assume that simply rejecting sin is enough — one must truly turn one's heart away from it.

sens: Aquatic bird considered unclean according to the law of Moses
Creature of the desert and ruins, symbol of desolation and solitude
H6893.detail:
1. The pelican is an aquatic bird that the law of Moses classifies among unclean animals, forbidden for consumption (Leviticus 11:18; Deuteronomy 14:17). It is a large water bird, recognizable by its characteristic silhouette, which the ancient Hebrews avoided as food just like the swan or the cormorant.
2. In prophetic visions, the pelican becomes the symbol of a devastated and abandoned place, populated only by wild beasts: the psalmist compares himself to the pelican of the desert to express his isolation and sadness (Psalms 102:7), while the prophets mention the pelican inhabiting the ruins to announce destruction and desolation (Isaiah 34:11; Zephaniah 2:14).
H6893.origine: The Hebrew word קָאַת (qa'at) refers to this aquatic bird, likely the pelican or a closely related species like the cormorant. Although the exact identification of the ancient animal is debated, the word is associated with a striking characteristic: it is a water bird that inhabits isolated and wild places. The Bible regularly juxtaposes it with other creatures of desert or ruined spaces.
H6893.emploi: This word appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, all in contexts that emphasize either ritual impurity or the image of desolation. In Leviticus 11:18 and Deuteronomy 14:17, it appears in lists of unclean birds, among other aquatic birds. From the psalms and the prophets (Psalms 102, Isaiah 34, Zephaniah 2), the pelican transcends its simple status as an unclean animal to become a poetic figure of ruin and mourning, inhabiting the collapsed columns of destroyed cities and symbolizing the end of a civilization.
H6893.portee: The pelican invites us to meditate on two realities: first, the holiness of God that separates the clean from the unclean in creation, reminding us that all that is created falls within His order. Secondly, through the image of the solitary pelican of the desert, we recognize how creatures and places become witnesses of divine justice that punishes sin; this image exhorts us to remain attached to God to avoid ruin.

sens: Animal excrement, particularly from birds
Material sold as food in times of extreme famine
H6894.detail:
1. Dung is the solid excretion of birds and other animals. In 2 Kings 6:25, it specifically refers to pigeon dung, mentioned in the horrifying context of the siege of Samaria.
2. In this same verse, dung becomes a food commodity exchanged for money during the great famine: a quarter of a kab (about 0.4 liters) cost five shekels of silver, while a donkey's head was worth eighty. This shows the extreme level of distress to which the besieged were reduced, consuming the disgusting.
H6894.origine: The Hebrew word קַב (qav) refers to a dry measure used for solids and grains. Here, it measures a quantity of dung. The word comes from a root that evokes a hollow or cavity (hence the meaning of 'measure'). The biblical context of 2 Kings 6 shows the use of the word to express a precise quantity of a substance reduced to the utmost degree of impurity and repugnance.
H6894.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Kings 6:25. It is found in a passage that describes the siege of Samaria by the Aramean army, where the famine became so terrible that the inhabitants consumed absolutely abominable things according to the Law: not only excrement but also donkey flesh. The context emphasizes the total collapse of social and religious order, the humiliation and ultimate despair of the people. The use of kab (a precise and known measure) with pigeon dung creates an ironic and chilling contrast: the impure is quantified like grain.
H6894.portee: This verse reminds us of the terrible consequences of sin, idolatry, and turning away from God, which bring divine judgment in the form of famine and siege. For the believer, it serves as a warning: abandoning God leads to unimaginable degradations. It is also a call to repentance, as the chapter later shows the miraculous deliverance sent by the Lord.

sens: To express against someone a word of curse, to wish harm upon them
To pronounce a judgment of condemnation
To be the object of a curse, to be cursed
H6895.detail: 1. To curse is to speak ill against a person, to hurl words of cursing so that they may be struck by misfortune. It is the act of one who, like Balaam, is summoned to 'curse' the people of Israel in Numbers 22:11: it is indeed about pronouncing against him words of condemnation. 2. The word also refers to the judgment of condemnation that strikes someone: in Proverbs 11:26, the one who withholds grain 'is cursed by the people', meaning struck by public disapproval and reproach. 3. Finally, to curse can simply mean 'to be cursed', to suffer the curse: in Job 3:8, it speaks of those 'who curse the days', that is, who cover them with a curse.
H6895.origine: The Hebrew verb קָבַב (qavav) expresses the action of pronouncing a curse, of covering someone with bad words. This word belongs to the family of terms for condemnation and cursing in Hebrew. It is distinct from the verb אָרַר (arar), which evokes rather the idea of cursing or binding by a curse with a deeper nuance of withering or ruin.
H6895.emploi: The verb קָבַב (to curse) appears about 12 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, primarily in the account of Balaam in Numbers 22-24, where Balak, king of Moab, implores the seer to curse Israel three times. Each time, Balaam refuses or is compelled to bless instead of curse. The word also appears in Job and Proverbs to express social or moral condemnation: the one who withholds grain is cursed by the people, those who curse the days suffer the consequences. The context always shows that cursing is a serious act, often vain or ineffective against the will of God.
H6895.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that words of cursing are never without weight, but that the curse of man can do nothing against the purposes of God. The account of Balaam teaches that no one can curse what God has blessed. This encourages the believer not to fear human curses and to place their trust in divine protection rather than in threats and words of condemnation.

sens: Cavity of the body containing the digestive system, between the esophagus and the intestine
Internal part of the animal offered in sacrifice
Belly or abdominal region
H6896.detail:
1. The stomach is the main organ of digestion, located in the belly of both humans and animals. It is a concrete, physical word that simply refers to this part of the body.

2. In the context of sacrifices, the stomach of the animal offered in sacrifice was a part reserved for the priest. In Deuteronomy 18:3, Moses lists what belongs to the priest: "the shoulder, the jaws, and the stomach." These portions of meat symbolized the priest's share in the sacrifice, a contribution from those who brought an animal to the Lord.

3. The word also more broadly refers to the belly or the interior of the body, as the seat of sensations or of what is digested.
H6896.origine: The Hebrew word קֵבָה comes from a root that evokes the idea of something hollow or enclosed. It belongs to the family of words designating parts of the human or animal body. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), the equivalent is found to describe the internal parts of the sacrificed animal, particularly those that were consecrated or distributed to the priests.
H6896.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Deuteronomy 18:3. It is found in the passage where Moses enumerates the rights of the priests over the people of Israel. This law specifies that when an ox or a lamb was offered in sacrifice, the priest received certain portions: the shoulder, the jaws, and the stomach. This portion was a mark of respect towards those who ensured worship to the Lord and served as intermediaries between God and the people.
H6896.portee: This passage reminds us that the priests, who dedicated their lives to serving God and instructing the people, were to be supported by the faithful through sacrifices. It is a lesson on fair sharing and honoring those who serve God. For the Christian, it also foreshadows that those who proclaim the Gospel have the right to live by the Gospel, as taught in the New Testament.

sens: The lower part of the belly, between the hips and the abdomen
In a sacrificed animal, the cavity of the belly where the internal organs are located
H6897.detail:
1. The lower abdomen is the region of the body that extends from the waist to the hips — the lowest part of the abdomen. It is the seat of vital and reproductive organs. In Numbers 25:8, the word specifically refers to the place where the spear pierces the body of an Israelite woman, thus indicating that it speaks of this precise area of the human body.
2. In sacrificed animals, the lower abdomen is the part where the entrails and viscera are found. It is in this region that the organs were to be examined to verify the quality of the victim offered to the Lord.
H6897.origine: The Hebrew word קֹבָה (qovah) specifically designates this cavity of the body. It belongs to the concrete vocabulary of human and animal anatomy, without any particular metaphorical imagery. It is a direct term for naming this part of the body.
H6897.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Numbers 25:8. It is the passage where the priest Phinehas puts an end to a scandal: he pierces an Israelite man and a Midianite woman with a spear, precisely through the lower abdomen. This context shows that the word unequivocally designates a visible and vulnerable part of the body.
H6897.portee: This passage reveals the dramatic stakes of sin: the lower abdomen, the seat of sexuality and reproduction, is also the seat of divine judgment against the guilty union. The reader understands that the Bible speaks of the body realistically, without evasion, and that infidelity towards God has tangible and serious consequences.

sens: Portable shelter made of fabric or skin, set up on a light framework
Among the Israelites, temporary dwelling in the desert or camp
In a figurative sense, dwelling or refuge
H6898.detail:
1. A tent is a dwelling made of fabric or skins stretched over a wooden or cord framework, easy to dismantle and transport. It is the typical habitat of nomads and people on the move, like the Israelites in the desert. In Numbers 25:8, it is in "his tent" that an Israelite retreats with a Midianite woman, meaning in the intimacy of his personal shelter.
2. The word also more broadly designates the temporary lodging of a traveler, soldier, or encampment. It is the place where one rests and lives day by day, as opposed to a house built of stone.
3. In a figurative or poetic sense, the word can evoke any dwelling, refuge, or asylum — the idea of being sheltered under something that protects you.
H6898.origine: The Hebrew word qoubba is a nominal form derived from a root that evokes the idea of arching or forming an arch. The name carries the image of a rounded, covered structure that envelops and protects. It is an ancient word, specific to the portable habitable structures of the peoples of the Levant and the desert.
H6898.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Numbers 25:8, in a passage of moral and religious crisis: an Israelite brings a Midianite woman into his tent, which provokes God's anger and an epidemic that decimates the people. Here, the tent is not simply a neutral shelter: it becomes the scene of a serious transgression of the command regarding mixed marriages and idolatry. The context reveals that the tent was the most private place, the intimate space of family life.
H6898.portee: This unique occurrence emphasizes how the tent, an everyday and ordinary shelter, can become the place where acts are committed that separate one from God. It reminds us that our private life, our choices of intimacy, are never out of God's sight, and that they have real spiritual consequences for the community we form with others. The tent embodies the vulnerability and nakedness of our existence before the Lord.

sens: A manufactured object that is worshiped as if it were a god
A collection of idols
That in which one places their trust instead of trusting in God
H6899.detail:
1. The word designates a manufactured object — statue, image, or representation — that is worshiped and prayed to as a god, even though it is merely a human creation. It is concretely the idol that people sculpt or mold to replace the true God (Isaiah 57:13).
2. The word can also refer to a crowd or a mass of idols, several statues gathered in one place: it conveys the idea of collection or assembly that gives its image to this word.
3. In a figurative sense, an idol is anything that one places in the place of God in their heart — wealth, power, reputation that one secretly adores. The prophet Isaiah sarcastically asks: can this crowd of idols save the one who worships them when danger comes? No: the wind will carry them away.
H6899.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to gather," "to assemble." The idol is thus originally the assembled object, crafted, collected by the hand of man. This is why the prophet insists: these are merely human creations gathered together, not divine powers that can save.
H6899.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 57:13. It is a passage of prophetic rebuke where Isaiah addresses the Israelites who have forsaken the Lord to worship the idols of neighboring peoples. The prophet highlights the absurdity of entrusting one's life to lifeless objects, fragile as leaves carried away by the wind. It is a contrast: these false gods can do nothing, while the one who trusts in the Lord will inherit the land and His holy mountain.
H6899.portee: This word calls the believer to examine their heart: what do they truly worship? Where do they place their trust on a daily basis? An idol is not always a stone statue; it is anything that takes the place of God — wealth, success, reputation, personal security. Isaiah teaches us that only trust in God brings true stability and eternal inheritance.

sens: Valley of Judah where a battle took place between Asa and the Ethiopian Zerah
H6859.detail: 1. Tsephata is a valley located in Judah, in the western region of the territory of Israel. Its name literally means "watchtower" or "observatory," evoking a high place from which one can survey the surroundings. In 2 Chronicles 14:9, King Asa confronts the army of Zerah the Ethiopian there: "Asa went out to meet him, and they drew up their battle lines in the valley of Tsephata, near Mareshah." It is in this place that God grants Asa victory despite the overwhelming numerical superiority of the enemy.
H6859.origine: The name Tsephata comes from the Hebrew root צפה (tsopha), which means "to observe," "to watch," or "to keep watch." This root evokes the idea of a height or a tower from which one surveys the horizon. The suffix -ה transforms the verb into a place name, as is common in biblical Hebrew to designate places characterized by a function or a topographical feature.
H6859.emploi: Tsephata appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 14:9. It is mentioned as the site of a major victory of King Asa of Judah against Zerah the Ethiopian. The precise location remains uncertain, but the text places it near Mareshah, in western Judah. This confrontation, where Asa cries out to God and receives miraculous deliverance, shows how God fights for His people when they put their trust in Him.
H6859.portee: This victory at Tsephata illustrates the biblical principle that trust in God and reliance on prayer are more valuable than military superiority. Asa, despite being overwhelmingly outnumbered, wins because he implores the Lord. This passage encourages the believer to trust God in seemingly desperate situations, knowing that He who observes from on high (like a watchtower) is stronger than any enemy.

sens: What comes out of the mouth of a person or an animal that vomits
State of one who vomits, action of vomiting
Filth, disgust, mark of humiliation
H6892B.detail:
1. Vomiting is primarily what comes out of the body when one vomits. In Isaiah 28:8, it speaks of tables full of vomit and filth: this is the rejected, abject, and repugnant matter that defiles whatever it touches.
2. The word also refers to the act of vomiting itself, the state of drunkenness or discomfort that provokes it. In Isaiah 19:14, a drunken man staggers "while vomiting": we see the image of a person deprived of reason and dignity.
3. Figuratively, vomiting becomes an image of humiliation and shame. In Jeremiah 48:26, Moab, who "rolls in his vomit," symbolizes the total humiliation of the people, reduced to the condition of an object of mockery and contempt.
H6892B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses violent rejection. It designates both physical vomiting and, by extension, what is rejected and abject. This strong image of rejection and disgust makes it a preferred term to express the idea of humiliation and moral degradation.
H6892B.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in the major prophets (Isaiah and Jeremiah). It is never used to simply describe a mundane medical phenomenon. On the contrary: Isaiah uses it to depict the drunkenness of the Egyptians and the ritual filth of profaned altars; Jeremiah uses it as an image of the humiliation of Moab in the face of God's judgment. The word always carries a charge of horror and contempt, associated with sin and its consequences.
H6892B.portee: Vomiting reminds us that sin produces a moral filth that disgusts God Himself. This raw and physical image makes divine judgment concrete: the man who rebels against God degrades himself, becoming repugnant. For the believer, it invites us to see sin not as a mere abstract transgression, but as something that truly defiles and humiliates.
